When God related this doubt of theirs, He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to answer this doubt by saying: ﴿Say: I am only a human like you, to whom it is revealed﴾. The explanation of this answer is as if he is saying: "I cannot compel you to faith by force and coercion. I am a human like you, and there is no distinction between me and you except merely that God, mighty and majestic, has revealed to me. What has been revealed to you, I convey this revelation to you. After that, if God honours you with monotheism and success, you will accept it, and if He forsakes you with deprivation, you will reject it; and that does not relate to my prophethood and my messengership." Then He explained that the essence of that revelation returns to two matters: knowledge and action. As for knowledge, the head and the chief of it is knowledge of monotheism (tawhid). This is because the truth is that God is one, and this is what is meant by His saying, ﴿that your God is one God﴾. Since the truth in itself is that, it is incumbent upon us to acknowledge it, and this is what is meant by His saying, ﴿so go straight to Him﴾. Its parallels are His saying, ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], and His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30], and His saying, ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153]. In His saying, ﴿so go straight to Him﴾, there are two aspects:

The first: "so be upright, turning toward Him."

The second: that His saying, "so go straight to Him," means "so be upright for Him," because some prepositions may stand in place of others.

Know that obligation (taklif) has two pillars: the first is belief, and its head and chief is belief in monotheism. Once He commanded this, He moved on to the duty of action, and the head and chief of it is seeking forgiveness. For this reason He said, ﴿and seek His forgiveness﴾. If it is said: the purpose of seeking forgiveness and repentance is the removal of what is not fitting, and that comes before doing what is fitting; so why did He reverse this order here and put what is fitting before the removal of what is not fitting? We say: the intended seeking of forgiveness here is not seeking forgiveness from disbelief. Rather, what is intended is that a person acts and then seeks forgiveness after it, out of fear of having fallen short in the action he performed, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, there is a veil over my heart, and indeed I seek forgiveness from God a hundred times a day" [reading as given: "seventy times"].

When God, exalted is He, encouraged goodness and obedience, He commanded warning against what is not fitting, so He said: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakah, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ In this verse there are issues:

Issue one: the aspects of the arrangement (wajh al-nazm) in this verse are several:

The first: the intellects and the sacred laws both affirm that the essence of felicities is tied to two matters: exalting the command of God, and compassion toward the creation of God. This is because existents are either the Creator or the created. As for the Creator, the perfection of felicity in dealing with Him is to acknowledge that He is described by the attributes of majesty and greatness, and then to perform acts that indicate that He is at the utmost greatness in our belief; and this is what is meant by exalting the command of God. As for the created, the perfection of felicity in dealing with them is to strive to repel evil from them and to bring good to them; and this is what is meant by compassion toward the creation of God. Thus it is established that the greatest acts of obedience are exalting the command of God, and the most excellent gates of exalting God's command is to affirm that He is one. When monotheism is the highest and noblest rank, its opposite, which is polytheism (shirk), is the lowest and basest rank. And since the most excellent kind of dealing with creation is to show compassion toward them, refraining from zakah is the basest of deeds, because it is the opposite of compassion toward the creation of God.

Knowing this, we say: He, exalted is He, established woe for one who is described by three attributes:

The first: that he is a polytheist, which is the opposite of monotheism, and to this points His saying, ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾.

The second: that he withholds zakah, which is the opposite of compassion toward the creation of God, and to this points His saying, ﴿who do not give zakah﴾.

The third: that he denies the Resurrection and is absorbed in seeking this world and its pleasures, and to this points His saying, ﴿and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾

The complete account on the fact that there are no more than these three levels is that a human being has three days: yesterday, today and tomorrow. As for knowing how the states of yesterday were in eternity, that is by knowing God, the Eternal, the Creator of this world. As for knowing how the states of today ought to occur, that is by doing good to the people of the world to the extent of one's capacity. As for knowing the states of the future day, that is affirming the Resurrection and the Last Day. When a person is opposed to the truth in these three levels, he is in the utmost ignorance and error, and for this reason God pronounced woe upon him, saying: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakah, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ This is an arrangement of the utmost excellence. And God knows best.

The second aspect in explaining the mode of the arrangement is to say: the meaning of His saying, ﴿who do not give zakah﴾ is: who do not purify themselves from the defilement of polytheism by saying "There is no god but God." This is taken from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ [al-Shams: 7].

[p. 87]

The third: al-Farra' said: the Quraysh used to feed the pilgrims, so they forbade that to whoever believed in Muhammad (ﷺ).

Issue two: Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) argued by this verse for establishing that the disbelievers are addressed with the branches of Islam (furu' al-Islam). They said: He, exalted is He, attached a severe threat based on two matters: the first being that he is a polytheist, and the second being that he does not give zakah. So each of these two matters must have an influence in bringing about that threat. This indicates that not giving zakah by a polytheist has a great influence in increasing the threat, and that is what was sought.

The third issue: Some scholars argued that refusing to give zakat (zakah, obligatory almsgiving) entails disbelief. They said: When God mentioned this attribute, He mentioned before it what entails disbelief, namely His saying ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾, and He also mentioned after it what entails disbelief, namely His saying ﴿and they are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers﴾. So if not giving zakat were not disbelief, then mentioning it between the two attributes that entail disbelief would be unseemly, because eloquent speech is only eloquent when the connection (munasabah) is observed between its parts. They reinforced this by saying that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, ruled that those who withheld zakat were disbelievers. The answer: Since it has been established by proof that faith (iman) is the affirmation of the heart and the verbal profession of the tongue, and both of these are present despite not giving zakat, it does not follow that disbelief results from not giving zakat. And Allah knows best.

Then, when God mentioned the threat against the disbelievers, He followed it with the promise to the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds will have a reward never to be cut off.﴾ That is, not cut off, from your saying "manantu al-habl" (I cut the rope), meaning I severed it, and from it their saying: "The journey has mannahu" (has cut him off), meaning it severed him. It was also said: [the meaning is] that it does not bestow favor (yamunnu) upon them, because when God called it a reward (ajr), then the reward does not necessitate obligation of favor. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the sick and the chronically disabled who, when they are unable to perform acts of obedience, are recorded for them the reward as the best of what they used to do.

[Page 81]

(Sūrat Fuṣṣilat)

Know that He, exalted is He, has passed judgment on the sūrah called "Ḥā Mīm" with several things:

The first is that it is a "tanzīl" (a revelation). The intended meaning is "munazzal" (that which was sent down). Using a verbal noun (maṣdar) to refer to a passive participle (maʿnā al-mafʿūl) is a well-known figurative usage (majāz). One says: "This is the building of the prince," meaning "its builder," and "This is the dirham, the minting of the sultan," meaning "its minted coin." The meaning of its being "tanzīl" is that God, exalted is He, wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ) and commanded Jibrīl (peace be upon him) to memorize those words, then descend with them upon Muḥammad (ﷺ) and convey them to him. When the understanding of these words was achieved through the descent of Jibrīl (peace be upon him), it was therefore called "tanzīl."

The second is that the revelation is "from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." This indicates that the revelation is a great blessing from God, exalted is He, because an act connected with a qualifier must be appropriate to that qualifier. Since His being "Raḥmān" and "Raḥīm" are two qualifiers that express the perfection of mercy, the revelation attributed to these two qualifiers must indicate the greatest aspects of blessing. The matter itself is indeed so, because creatures in this world are like the sick, the disabled and the needy. The Qur'an contains everything that the sick need of medicines and everything that the healthy need of foods. Therefore the greatest of the blessings of God, exalted is He, upon the people of this world is the sending down of the Qur'an to them.

The third is that it is a "Kitāb" (Book). We have already explained that this name is derived from "jamʿ" (gathering). It was called a "Kitāb" because it gathered within it the sciences of the former and the latter.

The fourth is His saying "﴿whose verses have been made distinct﴾." The meaning is that its verses have been separated and made into detailed explanations in different meanings. Some of them concern the description of the essence of God, exalted is He, and the explanation of the attributes of transcendence and sanctity, and the explanation of the perfection of His knowledge, power, mercy and wisdom, and the wonders of the states of His creation: the heavens, the earth, the stars, the alternation of night and day, and the wonders of the states of plants, animals and human beings. Some concern the states of the obligations directed toward the hearts and toward the limbs. Some concern promise and threat, reward and punishment, the ranks of the people of Paradise and the ranks of the people of Hell. Some concern admonitions and advice, some concern the refinement of character and the discipline of the soul, and some concern the stories of the former peoples and the histories of those who passed away.

In sum, whoever is fair will know that there is no book in the hands of creatures that has gathered within it such varied sciences and diverse subjects as the Qur'an has.

The fifth is His saying "﴿Qur'ān﴾." The reason for calling it "Qur'ān" has already been mentioned. His saying, exalted is He, "﴿Qur'ān﴾" is in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ) and praise, meaning: "By this distinct Book is intended a Qur'an whose attributes are such and such." It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

The sixth is His saying "﴿ʿarabiyyan﴾." The meaning is that this Qur'an was revealed only in the language of the Arabs. This is confirmed by His saying, exalted is He: "﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people﴾ [Ibrahim: 4]."

The seventh is His saying, exalted is He, "﴿for a people who know﴾." The meaning is: We made it Arabic because We sent it down to an Arab people, so We made it in the language of the Arabs so that they might understand its intended meaning. If it is asked: "What does His saying '﴿for a people who know﴾' relate to?" We reply: It may relate to "tanzīl" or to "fuṣṣilat," meaning: "a revelation from God for their sake," or "its verses have been made distinct for their sake." The better view is that it is a qualifier, like what comes before it and after it, meaning: "an Arabic Qur'an belonging to an Arab people," so that the relative clauses (ṣilāt) and the adjectives (ṣifāt) are not distinguished from one another.

The eighth and ninth: His saying "﴿a bearer of good news and a warner﴾." That is, a bearer of good news to the obedient with reward, and a warner to the wrongdoers with punishment. The truth is that the Qur'an is good news and warning, but the name of the agent was applied to it to draw attention to its being perfect in this attribute, just as one says "a poem that is poetic" (shiʿr shāʿir) and "a speech that is speaking" (kalām qāʾil).

The tenth attribute is that they turn away from it, do not listen, and do not pay attention to it. These are the ten attributes with which God described the Qur'an. Several questions branch out from these:

First question: Those who hold that the Qur'an is created argued from this verse in several ways.

The first: He described the Qur'an as being a "tanzīl" and "munazzal," and "munazzal" and "tanzīl" imply a transformation from one state to another. Therefore it must be created.

The second: "Tanzīl" is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and by the agreement of the grammarians, the verbal noun is the absolute object (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq).

The third: The meaning of "Kitāb" is either the act of writing, which is the absolute object, or the written thing, which is the object.

The fourth: His saying "﴿fuṣṣilat﴾" indicates that someone acts upon it by way of separating and distinguishing, and that does not befit the Eternal.

The fifth: It was called "Qur'ān" only because some of its parts were joined with others, and this indicates that it is an object made by a maker and a thing produced by one who produces.

The sixth: Describing it as "ʿarabiyyan." This attribution is valid only because these words entered upon these meanings according to the convention and terminology of the Arabs, and what is made by someone's making and someone's action must be originated and created.

The answer: All these points you have mentioned pertain to languages, letters and words, and these we also consider originated and created. What we claim to be eternal is something else apart from these words. And God knows best.

Second question: Most of the theologians (mutakallimūn) hold that it is obligatory for the responsible person to interpret the words of the Qur'an according to the meanings for which they were laid down in the Arabic language. As for carrying them to other meanings not by this method, that is certainly invalid. This is like the interpretations mentioned by the people of the esoteric (ahl al-bāṭin): sometimes they take the letters according to the reckoning of abjad (ḥisāb al-jummal), and sometimes they take each letter to refer to something else. The Sufis have many methods in this domain, and they call it "the science of unveiling" (ʿilm al-mukāshafah). What proves the invalidity of all those interpretations is His saying "﴿Qur'ān ʿarabiyyan﴾." He called it "ʿarabiyyan" only because it indicates these specific meanings by the convention and terminology of the Arabs. This indicates that the signification of these words was achieved only through those specific meanings, and that whatever is other than that is invalid.

Third question: Some people held that foreign languages occur in the Qur'an, such as His saying "﴿istabraq﴾" [al-Kahf: 31] and "﴿sijjīl﴾" [Hud: 82], which are Persian; and His saying "mishkāh" [al-Nur: 35], which is from the language of Abyssinia; and His saying "qisṭās" [al-Isra': 35], which is from the language of the Romans. What proves the invalidity of this view is His saying "﴿Qur'ān ʿarabiyyan﴾" and His saying "﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people﴾" [Ibrahim: 4].

Fourth question: The Mu'tazilah said that the terms "īmān" (faith), "kufr" (disbelief), "ṣalāh" (prayer), "zakāh" (almsgiving), "ṣawm" (fasting) and "ḥajj" (pilgrimage) are legal terms (alfāẓ sharʿiyyah), not linguistic ones. The meaning is that the Law transferred these words from their original linguistic referents to other referents. In our view, this is false. The Law has no power over these words to move them from their referents except in one respect: it restricted these names to one particular type of their referents. For example, "īmān" linguistically means assent (taṣdīq), and the Law restricted it to a specific kind of assent. "Ṣalāh" linguistically means supplication (duʿāʾ), and the Law restricted it to a specific kind of supplication. The same applies to the rest. Our proof of the soundness of our position is His saying "﴿Qur'ān ʿarabiyyan﴾" and His saying "﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people﴾."

* * *

Fifth question: God described the Qur'an as being "ʿarabiyyan" in the context of praise and glorification, and this aim is not achieved unless it is established that the language of the Arabs is the best of languages.

Know that this aim is achieved only if we fix the divisions of the excellences of languages by a known criterion, and then show that those divisions are present in it and not in anything else. So we say: Undoubtedly speech is composed of single words, and words are composed of letters. A word has a matter, which is the letters, and it has a form, which is that specific shape obtained through composition. This excellence is obtained either according to its matter or according to its form. As for what is according to its matter, it is the individual letters. Know that letters are of two kinds: some are clearly articulated in their points of articulation (makhārij) and clearly distinct in their boundaries, and some are obscure in their points of articulation and confused in their boundaries. All the letters of Arabic are clearly articulated and clearly distinct in their boundaries, and none of them is confused with another.

As for the letters used in other languages, they are not like this. Rather, a letter may occur in them that is confused with another, and that harms the completeness of eloquence (faṣāḥah). Also, the vowels used in the whole of the Arabic language are clear and manifest vowels, namely the accusative (naṣb), nominative (rafʿ) and genitive (jarr). Each of these three is distinguished from the others with a clear and manifest distinction. As for the ishmām and the rawm (partial vowel-coloring techniques), their occurrence is rare in Arabic dialects, and that too belongs to the category of things that produce eloquence.

As for the words that arise from composition, they are of several kinds:

The first: Letters are of two kinds: those whose points of articulation are close and those whose points of articulation are far apart. Also, letters are of two kinds: some are hard (ṣulbah) and some are soft (raxwah). From this division there arise four categories: hard and close, soft and close, hard and distant, soft and distant. When two hard letters with close points of articulation follow one another in a word, pronouncing it becomes difficult, because the closeness of the point of articulation makes its pronunciation like what happens when a person is shackled and then walks. And because of the hardness of those letters, strong and laborious actions converge on one point of articulation, and the succession of laborious actions causes weakness and exhaustion. Such a composition is rare in the Arabic language.

The second: The nature of some letters is sweeter and more pleasant to the hearing, and any word in which a letter of this nature occurs is more pleasant to hear.

Third: the metre (wazn). We say that a word is either biliteral, triliteral or quadriliteral, and the most balanced of these is the triliteral. This is because sound is only produced through movement, and movement must have a beginning, a middle and an end. These are three stages, so a word must contain these three stages in order to be complete. The biliteral is deficient, and the quadriliteral is excessive. What predominates in the speech of the Arabs are the triliterals. Thus, by what we have mentioned, the classification of the families of languages is established. Induction (istiqra') indicates that the language of the Arabs is characterised by this, whereas the other languages are not like this. And God knows best.

Issue six: His saying, ﴿for a people who know﴾, means: We made it Arabic only so that they might understand its meaning. Those who hold that God's acts are caused by benefits and wisdoms (al-mu'allilah bil-masalih wal-hikam) have relied on this verse and said: it indicates that He made it Arabic only for this wisdom. This shows that explaining God's acts and rulings by causes is permissible.

Issue seven: Some people said: the whole Qur'an is not known; rather, some of it is known and some of it is not. The theologians (al-mutakallimun) said: it is not permissible for there to be anything in it that is unknown. The evidence for this is His saying, ﴿a Book whose verses have been made clear, an Arabic Qur'an﴾, meaning: We made it Arabic only so that it would become known. To say that it is unknown is to cast doubt upon it.

Issue eight: His saying, ﴿but most of them turned away, so they do not hear﴾, indicates that the one who is guided is the one whom God guides, and the one who is astray is the one whom God leads astray. Its explanation is that the nine attributes mentioned for the Qur'an necessitate a strong concern for understanding it and for grasping its meanings. This is because we have shown that its being sent down from the God, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful, indicates that it contains the most excellent benefits and the most sublime aims; and its being ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾, detailed, indicates that it is in the utmost clarity and explanation; and its being ﴿a bringer of good news and a warner﴾ indicates that the need to understand what is in it is among the most important matters, because a person's striving to know what leads him to reward or to punishment is among the most important matters. These three necessitating factors have all been present, reinforcing the desire to understand the Qur'an and the strong inclination to encompass it. Nevertheless, they turned away from it, did not pay attention to it, and cast it behind their backs. This indicates

[p. 85]

that there is no one guided except the one whom God guides, and no one astray except the one whom God leads astray.

Know that when He, exalted is He, described the Qur'an by saying that they turned away from it and did not hear it, He then explained that they expressly declared this aversion and estrangement, and mentioned three things. The first: they said, ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to﴾. "Akinnah" is the plural of "kinan," like "aghiyah" is the plural of "ghita'," and the kinan is that in which arrows are placed.

The second: their saying, ﴿and in our ears is a deafness﴾, meaning deafness and heaviness from listening to your speech.

The third: their saying, ﴿and between us and you is a veil﴾. The "hijab" is that which prevents sight. The benefit of the word "min" in His saying, ﴿and between us﴾ is that if it had been said, "wa baynana wa baynaka hijab," the meaning would be that a veil had come to be in the middle between the two sides. But with the addition of the word "min," it is as if the meaning is that the veil began from us and began from you, so the distance between us and you is entirely filled by the veil, and no part of it remains empty of this veil. Thus this word indicates the strength of this veil. This is what the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned, and it is most excellent.

Know that the limitation to these three organs occurred because the heart is the locus of knowledge and the sovereign of the body, while the hearing and the sight are the two specific instruments for acquiring knowledge. So when He explained that these three were veiled, this was the utmost that can be achieved in this matter.

* * *

Know that when aversion from a thing becomes firm, that aversion settles in the heart; so when a person hears speech from it, he does not understand its meaning as it should be understood, and when he sees it, that sight does not become a means of comprehending the subtle details of that seen thing. The perceiver and the one who feels is the soul (nafs), and the intensity of the soul's aversion from a thing prevents it from reflecting on and comprehending the subtleties of that thing. When the matter is like this, their saying, ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is a deafness, and between us and you is a veil﴾ becomes complete metaphors (istiarat kamilah) in conveying the intended meaning.

If it is said: He, exalted is He, related this meaning from the unbelievers in a context of censure, and He also mentioned something close to it in a context of censure, saying: ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are uncircumcised." Rather, God has cursed them for their disbelief﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88].

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned these same three things in a context of affirmation and establishment in Surat al-An'am, saying: ﴿And We have placed coverings upon their hearts lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness﴾ [al-An'am: 25]. How then can these two be reconciled? We say: He did not say here that they lied in this. What He blamed them for is that they said: "If we are like this, then it is not permissible for us to be charged with obligation, nor for commands and prohibitions to be directed at us." And this second point is false. As for the first, there is nothing in the verse indicating that they lied in it.

Know that when they described themselves with these three attributes, they said, ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾. The meaning is: "Act according to your religion; indeed we are acting according to our religion." It is also possible that the meaning is: "Act in nullifying our affair; indeed we are acting in nullifying your affair." The conclusion for us is that the people did not lie in their saying, ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is a deafness, and between us and you is a veil﴾; rather, they uttered disbelief and false speech in their saying, ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾.

When God related this doubt of theirs, He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to answer this doubt by saying: ﴿Say: I am only a human like you, to whom it is revealed﴾. The explanation of this answer is as if he is saying: "I cannot compel you to faith by force and coercion. I am a human like you, and there is no distinction between me and you except merely that God, mighty and majestic, has revealed to me. What has been revealed to you, I convey this revelation to you. After that, if God honours you with monotheism and success, you will accept it, and if He forsakes you with deprivation, you will reject it; and that does not relate to my prophethood and my messengership." Then He explained that the essence of that revelation returns to two matters: knowledge and action. As for knowledge, the head and the chief of it is knowledge of monotheism (tawhid). This is because the truth is that God is one, and this is what is meant by His saying, ﴿that your God is one God﴾. Since the truth in itself is that, it is incumbent upon us to acknowledge it, and this is what is meant by His saying, ﴿so go straight to Him﴾. Its parallels are His saying, ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], and His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30], and His saying, ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153]. In His saying, ﴿so go straight to Him﴾, there are two aspects:

The first: "so be upright, turning toward Him."

The second: that His saying, "so go straight to Him," means "so be upright for Him," because some prepositions may stand in place of others.

Know that obligation (taklif) has two pillars: the first is belief, and its head and chief is belief in monotheism. Once He commanded this, He moved on to the duty of action, and the head and chief of it is seeking forgiveness. For this reason He said, ﴿and seek His forgiveness﴾. If it is said: the purpose of seeking forgiveness and repentance is the removal of what is not fitting, and that comes before doing what is fitting; so why did He reverse this order here and put what is fitting before the removal of what is not fitting? We say: the intended seeking of forgiveness here is not seeking forgiveness from disbelief. Rather, what is intended is that a person acts and then seeks forgiveness after it, out of fear of having fallen short in the action he performed, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, there is a veil over my heart, and indeed I seek forgiveness from God a hundred times a day" [reading as given: "seventy times"].

When God, exalted is He, encouraged goodness and obedience, He commanded warning against what is not fitting, so He said: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakah, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ In this verse there are issues:

Issue one: the aspects of the arrangement (wajh al-nazm) in this verse are several:

The first: the intellects and the sacred laws both affirm that the essence of felicities is tied to two matters: exalting the command of God, and compassion toward the creation of God. This is because existents are either the Creator or the created. As for the Creator, the perfection of felicity in dealing with Him is to acknowledge that He is described by the attributes of majesty and greatness, and then to perform acts that indicate that He is at the utmost greatness in our belief; and this is what is meant by exalting the command of God. As for the created, the perfection of felicity in dealing with them is to strive to repel evil from them and to bring good to them; and this is what is meant by compassion toward the creation of God. Thus it is established that the greatest acts of obedience are exalting the command of God, and the most excellent gates of exalting God's command is to affirm that He is one. When monotheism is the highest and noblest rank, its opposite, which is polytheism (shirk), is the lowest and basest rank. And since the most excellent kind of dealing with creation is to show compassion toward them, refraining from zakah is the basest of deeds, because it is the opposite of compassion toward the creation of God.

Knowing this, we say: He, exalted is He, established woe for one who is described by three attributes:

The first: that he is a polytheist, which is the opposite of monotheism, and to this points His saying, ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾.

The second: that he withholds zakah, which is the opposite of compassion toward the creation of God, and to this points His saying, ﴿who do not give zakah﴾.

The third: that he denies the Resurrection and is absorbed in seeking this world and its pleasures, and to this points His saying, ﴿and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾

The complete account on the fact that there are no more than these three levels is that a human being has three days: yesterday, today and tomorrow. As for knowing how the states of yesterday were in eternity, that is by knowing God, the Eternal, the Creator of this world. As for knowing how the states of today ought to occur, that is by doing good to the people of the world to the extent of one's capacity. As for knowing the states of the future day, that is affirming the Resurrection and the Last Day. When a person is opposed to the truth in these three levels, he is in the utmost ignorance and error, and for this reason God pronounced woe upon him, saying: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakah, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ This is an arrangement of the utmost excellence. And God knows best.

The second aspect in explaining the mode of the arrangement is to say: the meaning of His saying, ﴿who do not give zakah﴾ is: who do not purify themselves from the defilement of polytheism by saying "There is no god but God." This is taken from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ [al-Shams: 7].

[p. 87]

The third: al-Farra' said: the Quraysh used to feed the pilgrims, so they forbade that to whoever believed in Muhammad (ﷺ).

Issue two: Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) argued by this verse for establishing that the disbelievers are addressed with the branches of Islam (furu' al-Islam). They said: He, exalted is He, attached a severe threat based on two matters: the first being that he is a polytheist, and the second being that he does not give zakah. So each of these two matters must have an influence in bringing about that threat. This indicates that not giving zakah by a polytheist has a great influence in increasing the threat, and that is what was sought.

The third issue: Some scholars argued that refusing to give zakat (zakah, obligatory almsgiving) entails disbelief. They said: When God mentioned this attribute, He mentioned before it what entails disbelief, namely His saying ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾, and He also mentioned after it what entails disbelief, namely His saying ﴿and they are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers﴾. So if not giving zakat were not disbelief, then mentioning it between the two attributes that entail disbelief would be unseemly, because eloquent speech is only eloquent when the connection (munasabah) is observed between its parts. They reinforced this by saying that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, ruled that those who withheld zakat were disbelievers. The answer: Since it has been established by proof that faith (iman) is the affirmation of the heart and the verbal profession of the tongue, and both of these are present despite not giving zakat, it does not follow that disbelief results from not giving zakat. And Allah knows best.

Then, when God mentioned the threat against the disbelievers, He followed it with the promise to the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds will have a reward never to be cut off.﴾ That is, not cut off, from your saying "manantu al-habl" (I cut the rope), meaning I severed it, and from it their saying: "The journey has mannahu" (has cut him off), meaning it severed him. It was also said: [the meaning is] that it does not bestow favor (yamunnu) upon them, because when God called it a reward (ajr), then the reward does not necessitate obligation of favor. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the sick and the chronically disabled who, when they are unable to perform acts of obedience, are recorded for them the reward as the best of what they used to do.

[Page 81]

(Sūrat Fuṣṣilat)
Fifty-four verses, Meccan

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ḥā Mīm.﴾ ﴿A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿A Book whose verses have been made distinct, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know.﴾ ﴿A bearer of good news and a warner, yet most of them turn away, so they do not listen.﴾ ﴿They say, "Our hearts are under coverings from that to which you call us, and there is deafness in our ears, and between us and you there is a barrier. So act, for we are acting."﴾ ﴿Say, "I am only a human being like you. It has been revealed to me that your God is one God. So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness. And woe to the polytheists,﴾ ﴿who do not give the zakat and who disbelieve in the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward that will never be cut off.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ḥā Mīm.﴾ ﴿A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿A Book whose verses have been made distinct, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know.﴾ ﴿A bearer of good news and a warner, yet most of them turn away, so they do not listen.﴾ ﴿They say, "Our hearts are under coverings from that to which you call us, and there is deafness in our ears, and between us and you there is a barrier. So act, for we are acting."﴾ ﴿Say, "I am only a human being like you. It has been revealed to me that your God is one God. So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness. And woe to the polytheists,﴾ ﴿who do not give the zakat and who disbelieve in the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward that will never be cut off.﴾

Know that at the beginning of this sūrah there are several possibilities. The first, which is the strongest, is that one says "Ḥā Mīm" is the name of the sūrah and is in the position of the subject (mubtadaʾ), and "tanzīl" (a revelation) is its predicate (khabar). The second: al-Akhfash said that "tanzīl" is in the nominative by being the subject, and "Kitāb" is its predicate. The third: al-Zajjāj said that "tanzīl" is in the nominative as a subject, and its predicate is "﴿a Book whose verses have been made distinct﴾." Its justification is that the word "tanzīl" has been specified by the qualifier, which is "﴿from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾," and so it was permissible for it to occur as a subject.

[Page 82]

Know that He, exalted is He, has passed judgment on the sūrah called "Ḥā Mīm" with several things:

The first is that it is a "tanzīl" (a revelation). The intended meaning is "munazzal" (that which was sent down). Using a verbal noun (maṣdar) to refer to a passive participle (maʿnā al-mafʿūl) is a well-known figurative usage (majāz). One says: "This is the building of the prince," meaning "its builder," and "This is the dirham, the minting of the sultan," meaning "its minted coin." The meaning of its being "tanzīl" is that God, exalted is He, wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ) and commanded Jibrīl (peace be upon him) to memorize those words, then descend with them upon Muḥammad (ﷺ) and convey them to him. When the understanding of these words was achieved through the descent of Jibrīl (peace be upon him), it was therefore called "tanzīl."

The second is that the revelation is "from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." This indicates that the revelation is a great blessing from God, exalted is He, because an act connected with a qualifier must be appropriate to that qualifier. Since His being "Raḥmān" and "Raḥīm" are two qualifiers that express the perfection of mercy, the revelation attributed to these two qualifiers must indicate the greatest aspects of blessing. The matter itself is indeed so, because creatures in this world are like the sick, the disabled and the needy. The Qur'an contains everything that the sick need of medicines and everything that the healthy need of foods. Therefore the greatest of the blessings of God, exalted is He, upon the people of this world is the sending down of the Qur'an to them.

The third is that it is a "Kitāb" (Book). We have already explained that this name is derived from "jamʿ" (gathering). It was called a "Kitāb" because it gathered within it the sciences of the former and the latter.

The fourth is His saying "﴿whose verses have been made distinct﴾." The meaning is that its verses have been separated and made into detailed explanations in different meanings. Some of them concern the description of the essence of God, exalted is He, and the explanation of the attributes of transcendence and sanctity, and the explanation of the perfection of His knowledge, power, mercy and wisdom, and the wonders of the states of His creation: the heavens, the earth, the stars, the alternation of night and day, and the wonders of the states of plants, animals and human beings. Some concern the states of the obligations directed toward the hearts and toward the limbs. Some concern promise and threat, reward and punishment, the ranks of the people of Paradise and the ranks of the people of Hell. Some concern admonitions and advice, some concern the refinement of character and the discipline of the soul, and some concern the stories of the former peoples and the histories of those who passed away.

In sum, whoever is fair will know that there is no book in the hands of creatures that has gathered within it such varied sciences and diverse subjects as the Qur'an has.

The fifth is His saying "﴿Qur'ān﴾." The reason for calling it "Qur'ān" has already been mentioned. His saying, exalted is He, "﴿Qur'ān﴾" is in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ) and praise, meaning: "By this distinct Book is intended a Qur'an whose attributes are such and such." It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

The sixth is His saying "﴿ʿarabiyyan﴾." The meaning is that this Qur'an was revealed only in the language of the Arabs. This is confirmed by His saying, exalted is He: "﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people﴾ [Ibrahim: 4]."

The seventh is His saying, exalted is He, "﴿for a people who know﴾." The meaning is: We made it Arabic because We sent it down to an Arab people, so We made it in the language of the Arabs so that they might understand its intended meaning. If it is asked: "What does His saying '﴿for a people who know﴾' relate to?" We reply: It may relate to "tanzīl" or to "fuṣṣilat," meaning: "a revelation from God for their sake," or "its verses have been made distinct for their sake." The better view is that it is a qualifier, like what comes before it and after it, meaning: "an Arabic Qur'an belonging to an Arab people," so that the relative clauses (ṣilāt) and the adjectives (ṣifāt) are not distinguished from one another.

The eighth and ninth: His saying "﴿a bearer of good news and a warner﴾." That is, a bearer of good news to the obedient with reward, and a warner to the wrongdoers with punishment. The truth is that the Qur'an is good news and warning, but the name of the agent was applied to it to draw attention to its being perfect in this attribute, just as one says "a poem that is poetic" (shiʿr shāʿir) and "a speech that is speaking" (kalām qāʾil).

The tenth attribute is that they turn away from it, do not listen, and do not pay attention to it. These are the ten attributes with which God described the Qur'an. Several questions branch out from these:

First question: Those who hold that the Qur'an is created argued from this verse in several ways.

The first: He described the Qur'an as being a "tanzīl" and "munazzal," and "munazzal" and "tanzīl" imply a transformation from one state to another. Therefore it must be created.

The second: "Tanzīl" is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and by the agreement of the grammarians, the verbal noun is the absolute object (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq).

The third: The meaning of "Kitāb" is either the act of writing, which is the absolute object, or the written thing, which is the object.

The fourth: His saying "﴿fuṣṣilat﴾" indicates that someone acts upon it by way of separating and distinguishing, and that does not befit the Eternal.

The fifth: It was called "Qur'ān" only because some of its parts were joined with others, and this indicates that it is an object made by a maker and a thing produced by one who produces.

The sixth: Describing it as "ʿarabiyyan." This attribution is valid only because these words entered upon these meanings according to the convention and terminology of the Arabs, and what is made by someone's making and someone's action must be originated and created.

The answer: All these points you have mentioned pertain to languages, letters and words, and these we also consider originated and created. What we claim to be eternal is something else apart from these words. And God knows best.

Second question: Most of the theologians (mutakallimūn) hold that it is obligatory for the responsible person to interpret the words of the Qur'an according to the meanings for which they were laid down in the Arabic language. As for carrying them to other meanings not by this method, that is certainly invalid. This is like the interpretations mentioned by the people of the esoteric (ahl al-bāṭin): sometimes they take the letters according to the reckoning of abjad (ḥisāb al-jummal), and sometimes they take each letter to refer to something else. The Sufis have many methods in this domain, and they call it "the science of unveiling" (ʿilm al-mukāshafah). What proves the invalidity of all those interpretations is His saying "﴿Qur'ān ʿarabiyyan﴾." He called it "ʿarabiyyan" only because it indicates these specific meanings by the convention and terminology of the Arabs. This indicates that the signification of these words was achieved only through those specific meanings, and that whatever is other than that is invalid.

Third question: Some people held that foreign languages occur in the Qur'an, such as His saying "﴿istabraq﴾" [al-Kahf: 31] and "﴿sijjīl﴾" [Hud: 82], which are Persian; and His saying "mishkāh" [al-Nur: 35], which is from the language of Abyssinia; and His saying "qisṭās" [al-Isra': 35], which is from the language of the Romans. What proves the invalidity of this view is His saying "﴿Qur'ān ʿarabiyyan﴾" and His saying "﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people﴾" [Ibrahim: 4].

Fourth question: The Mu'tazilah said that the terms "īmān" (faith), "kufr" (disbelief), "ṣalāh" (prayer), "zakāh" (almsgiving), "ṣawm" (fasting) and "ḥajj" (pilgrimage) are legal terms (alfāẓ sharʿiyyah), not linguistic ones. The meaning is that the Law transferred these words from their original linguistic referents to other referents. In our view, this is false. The Law has no power over these words to move them from their referents except in one respect: it restricted these names to one particular type of their referents. For example, "īmān" linguistically means assent (taṣdīq), and the Law restricted it to a specific kind of assent. "Ṣalāh" linguistically means supplication (duʿāʾ), and the Law restricted it to a specific kind of supplication. The same applies to the rest. Our proof of the soundness of our position is His saying "﴿Qur'ān ʿarabiyyan﴾" and His saying "﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people﴾."

* * *

Fifth question: God described the Qur'an as being "ʿarabiyyan" in the context of praise and glorification, and this aim is not achieved unless it is established that the language of the Arabs is the best of languages.

Know that this aim is achieved only if we fix the divisions of the excellences of languages by a known criterion, and then show that those divisions are present in it and not in anything else. So we say: Undoubtedly speech is composed of single words, and words are composed of letters. A word has a matter, which is the letters, and it has a form, which is that specific shape obtained through composition. This excellence is obtained either according to its matter or according to its form. As for what is according to its matter, it is the individual letters. Know that letters are of two kinds: some are clearly articulated in their points of articulation (makhārij) and clearly distinct in their boundaries, and some are obscure in their points of articulation and confused in their boundaries. All the letters of Arabic are clearly articulated and clearly distinct in their boundaries, and none of them is confused with another.

As for the letters used in other languages, they are not like this. Rather, a letter may occur in them that is confused with another, and that harms the completeness of eloquence (faṣāḥah). Also, the vowels used in the whole of the Arabic language are clear and manifest vowels, namely the accusative (naṣb), nominative (rafʿ) and genitive (jarr). Each of these three is distinguished from the others with a clear and manifest distinction. As for the ishmām and the rawm (partial vowel-coloring techniques), their occurrence is rare in Arabic dialects, and that too belongs to the category of things that produce eloquence.

As for the words that arise from composition, they are of several kinds:

The first: Letters are of two kinds: those whose points of articulation are close and those whose points of articulation are far apart. Also, letters are of two kinds: some are hard (ṣulbah) and some are soft (raxwah). From this division there arise four categories: hard and close, soft and close, hard and distant, soft and distant. When two hard letters with close points of articulation follow one another in a word, pronouncing it becomes difficult, because the closeness of the point of articulation makes its pronunciation like what happens when a person is shackled and then walks. And because of the hardness of those letters, strong and laborious actions converge on one point of articulation, and the succession of laborious actions causes weakness and exhaustion. Such a composition is rare in the Arabic language.

The second: The nature of some letters is sweeter and more pleasant to the hearing, and any word in which a letter of this nature occurs is more pleasant to hear.

Third: the metre (wazn). We say that a word is either biliteral, triliteral or quadriliteral, and the most balanced of these is the triliteral. This is because sound is only produced through movement, and movement must have a beginning, a middle and an end. These are three stages, so a word must contain these three stages in order to be complete. The biliteral is deficient, and the quadriliteral is excessive. What predominates in the speech of the Arabs are the triliterals. Thus, by what we have mentioned, the classification of the families of languages is established. Induction (istiqra') indicates that the language of the Arabs is characterised by this, whereas the other languages are not like this. And God knows best.

Issue six: His saying, ﴿for a people who know﴾, means: We made it Arabic only so that they might understand its meaning. Those who hold that God's acts are caused by benefits and wisdoms (al-mu'allilah bil-masalih wal-hikam) have relied on this verse and said: it indicates that He made it Arabic only for this wisdom. This shows that explaining God's acts and rulings by causes is permissible.

Issue seven: Some people said: the whole Qur'an is not known; rather, some of it is known and some of it is not. The theologians (al-mutakallimun) said: it is not permissible for there to be anything in it that is unknown. The evidence for this is His saying, ﴿a Book whose verses have been made clear, an Arabic Qur'an﴾, meaning: We made it Arabic only so that it would become known. To say that it is unknown is to cast doubt upon it.

Issue eight: His saying, ﴿but most of them turned away, so they do not hear﴾, indicates that the one who is guided is the one whom God guides, and the one who is astray is the one whom God leads astray. Its explanation is that the nine attributes mentioned for the Qur'an necessitate a strong concern for understanding it and for grasping its meanings. This is because we have shown that its being sent down from the God, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful, indicates that it contains the most excellent benefits and the most sublime aims; and its being ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾, detailed, indicates that it is in the utmost clarity and explanation; and its being ﴿a bringer of good news and a warner﴾ indicates that the need to understand what is in it is among the most important matters, because a person's striving to know what leads him to reward or to punishment is among the most important matters. These three necessitating factors have all been present, reinforcing the desire to understand the Qur'an and the strong inclination to encompass it. Nevertheless, they turned away from it, did not pay attention to it, and cast it behind their backs. This indicates

[p. 85]

that there is no one guided except the one whom God guides, and no one astray except the one whom God leads astray.

Know that when He, exalted is He, described the Qur'an by saying that they turned away from it and did not hear it, He then explained that they expressly declared this aversion and estrangement, and mentioned three things. The first: they said, ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to﴾. "Akinnah" is the plural of "kinan," like "aghiyah" is the plural of "ghita'," and the kinan is that in which arrows are placed.

The second: their saying, ﴿and in our ears is a deafness﴾, meaning deafness and heaviness from listening to your speech.

The third: their saying, ﴿and between us and you is a veil﴾. The "hijab" is that which prevents sight. The benefit of the word "min" in His saying, ﴿and between us﴾ is that if it had been said, "wa baynana wa baynaka hijab," the meaning would be that a veil had come to be in the middle between the two sides. But with the addition of the word "min," it is as if the meaning is that the veil began from us and began from you, so the distance between us and you is entirely filled by the veil, and no part of it remains empty of this veil. Thus this word indicates the strength of this veil. This is what the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned, and it is most excellent.

Know that the limitation to these three organs occurred because the heart is the locus of knowledge and the sovereign of the body, while the hearing and the sight are the two specific instruments for acquiring knowledge. So when He explained that these three were veiled, this was the utmost that can be achieved in this matter.

* * *

Know that when aversion from a thing becomes firm, that aversion settles in the heart; so when a person hears speech from it, he does not understand its meaning as it should be understood, and when he sees it, that sight does not become a means of comprehending the subtle details of that seen thing. The perceiver and the one who feels is the soul (nafs), and the intensity of the soul's aversion from a thing prevents it from reflecting on and comprehending the subtleties of that thing. When the matter is like this, their saying, ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is a deafness, and between us and you is a veil﴾ becomes complete metaphors (istiarat kamilah) in conveying the intended meaning.

If it is said: He, exalted is He, related this meaning from the unbelievers in a context of censure, and He also mentioned something close to it in a context of censure, saying: ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are uncircumcised." Rather, God has cursed them for their disbelief﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88].

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned these same three things in a context of affirmation and establishment in Surat al-An'am, saying: ﴿And We have placed coverings upon their hearts lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness﴾ [al-An'am: 25]. How then can these two be reconciled? We say: He did not say here that they lied in this. What He blamed them for is that they said: "If we are like this, then it is not permissible for us to be charged with obligation, nor for commands and prohibitions to be directed at us." And this second point is false. As for the first, there is nothing in the verse indicating that they lied in it.

Know that when they described themselves with these three attributes, they said, ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾. The meaning is: "Act according to your religion; indeed we are acting according to our religion." It is also possible that the meaning is: "Act in nullifying our affair; indeed we are acting in nullifying your affair." The conclusion for us is that the people did not lie in their saying, ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is a deafness, and between us and you is a veil﴾; rather, they uttered disbelief and false speech in their saying, ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾.

When God related this doubt of theirs, He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to answer this doubt by saying: ﴿Say: I am only a human like you, to whom it is revealed﴾. The explanation of this answer is as if he is saying: "I cannot compel you to faith by force and coercion. I am a human like you, and there is no distinction between me and you except merely that God, mighty and majestic, has revealed to me. What has been revealed to you, I convey this revelation to you. After that, if God honours you with monotheism and success, you will accept it, and if He forsakes you with deprivation, you will reject it; and that does not relate to my prophethood and my messengership." Then He explained that the essence of that revelation returns to two matters: knowledge and action. As for knowledge, the head and the chief of it is knowledge of monotheism (tawhid). This is because the truth is that God is one, and this is what is meant by His saying, ﴿that your God is one God﴾. Since the truth in itself is that, it is incumbent upon us to acknowledge it, and this is what is meant by His saying, ﴿so go straight to Him﴾. Its parallels are His saying, ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], and His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30], and His saying, ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153]. In His saying, ﴿so go straight to Him﴾, there are two aspects:

The first: "so be upright, turning toward Him."

The second: that His saying, "so go straight to Him," means "so be upright for Him," because some prepositions may stand in place of others.

Know that obligation (taklif) has two pillars: the first is belief, and its head and chief is belief in monotheism. Once He commanded this, He moved on to the duty of action, and the head and chief of it is seeking forgiveness. For this reason He said, ﴿and seek His forgiveness﴾. If it is said: the purpose of seeking forgiveness and repentance is the removal of what is not fitting, and that comes before doing what is fitting; so why did He reverse this order here and put what is fitting before the removal of what is not fitting? We say: the intended seeking of forgiveness here is not seeking forgiveness from disbelief. Rather, what is intended is that a person acts and then seeks forgiveness after it, out of fear of having fallen short in the action he performed, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, there is a veil over my heart, and indeed I seek forgiveness from God a hundred times a day" [reading as given: "seventy times"].

When God, exalted is He, encouraged goodness and obedience, He commanded warning against what is not fitting, so He said: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakah, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ In this verse there are issues:

Issue one: the aspects of the arrangement (wajh al-nazm) in this verse are several:

The first: the intellects and the sacred laws both affirm that the essence of felicities is tied to two matters: exalting the command of God, and compassion toward the creation of God. This is because existents are either the Creator or the created. As for the Creator, the perfection of felicity in dealing with Him is to acknowledge that He is described by the attributes of majesty and greatness, and then to perform acts that indicate that He is at the utmost greatness in our belief; and this is what is meant by exalting the command of God. As for the created, the perfection of felicity in dealing with them is to strive to repel evil from them and to bring good to them; and this is what is meant by compassion toward the creation of God. Thus it is established that the greatest acts of obedience are exalting the command of God, and the most excellent gates of exalting God's command is to affirm that He is one. When monotheism is the highest and noblest rank, its opposite, which is polytheism (shirk), is the lowest and basest rank. And since the most excellent kind of dealing with creation is to show compassion toward them, refraining from zakah is the basest of deeds, because it is the opposite of compassion toward the creation of God.

Knowing this, we say: He, exalted is He, established woe for one who is described by three attributes:

The first: that he is a polytheist, which is the opposite of monotheism, and to this points His saying, ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾.

The second: that he withholds zakah, which is the opposite of compassion toward the creation of God, and to this points His saying, ﴿who do not give zakah﴾.

The third: that he denies the Resurrection and is absorbed in seeking this world and its pleasures, and to this points His saying, ﴿and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾

The complete account on the fact that there are no more than these three levels is that a human being has three days: yesterday, today and tomorrow. As for knowing how the states of yesterday were in eternity, that is by knowing God, the Eternal, the Creator of this world. As for knowing how the states of today ought to occur, that is by doing good to the people of the world to the extent of one's capacity. As for knowing the states of the future day, that is affirming the Resurrection and the Last Day. When a person is opposed to the truth in these three levels, he is in the utmost ignorance and error, and for this reason God pronounced woe upon him, saying: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakah, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ This is an arrangement of the utmost excellence. And God knows best.

The second aspect in explaining the mode of the arrangement is to say: the meaning of His saying, ﴿who do not give zakah﴾ is: who do not purify themselves from the defilement of polytheism by saying "There is no god but God." This is taken from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ [al-Shams: 7].

[p. 87]

The third: al-Farra' said: the Quraysh used to feed the pilgrims, so they forbade that to whoever believed in Muhammad (ﷺ).

Issue two: Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) argued by this verse for establishing that the disbelievers are addressed with the branches of Islam (furu' al-Islam). They said: He, exalted is He, attached a severe threat based on two matters: the first being that he is a polytheist, and the second being that he does not give zakah. So each of these two matters must have an influence in bringing about that threat. This indicates that not giving zakah by a polytheist has a great influence in increasing the threat, and that is what was sought.

The third issue: Some scholars argued that refusing to give zakat (zakah, obligatory almsgiving) entails disbelief. They said: When God mentioned this attribute, He mentioned before it what entails disbelief, namely His saying ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾, and He also mentioned after it what entails disbelief, namely His saying ﴿and they are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers﴾. So if not giving zakat were not disbelief, then mentioning it between the two attributes that entail disbelief would be unseemly, because eloquent speech is only eloquent when the connection (munasabah) is observed between its parts. They reinforced this by saying that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, ruled that those who withheld zakat were disbelievers. The answer: Since it has been established by proof that faith (iman) is the affirmation of the heart and the verbal profession of the tongue, and both of these are present despite not giving zakat, it does not follow that disbelief results from not giving zakat. And Allah knows best.

Then, when God mentioned the threat against the disbelievers, He followed it with the promise to the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds will have a reward never to be cut off.﴾ That is, not cut off, from your saying "manantu al-habl" (I cut the rope), meaning I severed it, and from it their saying: "The journey has mannahu" (has cut him off), meaning it severed him. It was also said: [the meaning is] that it does not bestow favor (yamunnu) upon them, because when God called it a reward (ajr), then the reward does not necessitate obligation of favor. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the sick and the chronically disabled who, when they are unable to perform acts of obedience, are recorded for them the reward as the best of what they used to do.

[Page 81]

(Sūrat Fuṣṣilat)
Fifty-four verses, Meccan

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ḥā Mīm.﴾ ﴿A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿A Book whose verses have been made distinct, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know.﴾ ﴿A bearer of good news and a warner, yet most of them turn away, so they do not listen.﴾ ﴿They say, "Our hearts are under coverings from that to which you call us, and there is deafness in our ears, and between us and you there is a barrier. So act, for we are acting."﴾ ﴿Say, "I am only a human being like you. It has been revealed to me that your God is one God. So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness. And woe to the polytheists,﴾ ﴿who do not give the zakat and who disbelieve in the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward that will never be cut off.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ḥā Mīm.﴾ ﴿A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿A Book whose verses have been made distinct, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know.﴾ ﴿A bearer of good news and a warner, yet most of them turn away, so they do not listen.﴾ ﴿They say, "Our hearts are under coverings from that to which you call us, and there is deafness in our ears, and between us and you there is a barrier. So act, for we are acting."﴾ ﴿Say, "I am only a human being like you. It has been revealed to me that your God is one God. So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness. And woe to the polytheists,﴾ ﴿who do not give the zakat and who disbelieve in the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward that will never be cut off.﴾

Know that at the beginning of this sūrah there are several possibilities. The first, which is the strongest, is that one says "Ḥā Mīm" is the name of the sūrah and is in the position of the subject (mubtadaʾ), and "tanzīl" (a revelation) is its predicate (khabar). The second: al-Akhfash said that "tanzīl" is in the nominative by being the subject, and "Kitāb" is its predicate. The third: al-Zajjāj said that "tanzīl" is in the nominative as a subject, and its predicate is "﴿a Book whose verses have been made distinct﴾." Its justification is that the word "tanzīl" has been specified by the qualifier, which is "﴿from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾," and so it was permissible for it to occur as a subject.

[Page 82]

Know that He, exalted is He, has passed judgment on the sūrah called "Ḥā Mīm" with several things:

The first is that it is a "tanzīl" (a revelation). The intended meaning is "munazzal" (that which was sent down). Using a verbal noun (maṣdar) to refer to a passive participle (maʿnā al-mafʿūl) is a well-known figurative usage (majāz). One says: "This is the building of the prince," meaning "its builder," and "This is the dirham, the minting of the sultan," meaning "its minted coin." The meaning of its being "tanzīl" is that God, exalted is He, wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ) and commanded Jibrīl (peace be upon him) to memorize those words, then descend with them upon Muḥammad (ﷺ) and convey them to him. When the understanding of these words was achieved through the descent of Jibrīl (peace be upon him), it was therefore called "tanzīl."

The second is that the revelation is "from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." This indicates that the revelation is a great blessing from God, exalted is He, because an act connected with a qualifier must be appropriate to that qualifier. Since His being "Raḥmān" and "Raḥīm" are two qualifiers that express the perfection of mercy, the revelation attributed to these two qualifiers must indicate the greatest aspects of blessing. The matter itself is indeed so, because creatures in this world are like the sick, the disabled and the needy. The Qur'an contains everything that the sick need of medicines and everything that the healthy need of foods. Therefore the greatest of the blessings of God, exalted is He, upon the people of this world is the sending down of the Qur'an to them.

The third is that it is a "Kitāb" (Book). We have already explained that this name is derived from "jamʿ" (gathering). It was called a "Kitāb" because it gathered within it the sciences of the former and the latter.

The fourth is His saying "﴿whose verses have been made distinct﴾." The meaning is that its verses have been separated and made into detailed explanations in different meanings. Some of them concern the description of the essence of God, exalted is He, and the explanation of the attributes of transcendence and sanctity, and the explanation of the perfection of His knowledge, power, mercy and wisdom, and the wonders of the states of His creation: the heavens, the earth, the stars, the alternation of night and day, and the wonders of the states of plants, animals and human beings. Some concern the states of the obligations directed toward the hearts and toward the limbs. Some concern promise and threat, reward and punishment, the ranks of the people of Paradise and the ranks of the people of Hell. Some concern admonitions and advice, some concern the refinement of character and the discipline of the soul, and some concern the stories of the former peoples and the histories of those who passed away.

In sum, whoever is fair will know that there is no book in the hands of creatures that has gathered within it such varied sciences and diverse subjects as the Qur'an has.

The fifth is His saying "﴿Qur'ān﴾." The reason for calling it "Qur'ān" has already been mentioned. His saying, exalted is He, "﴿Qur'ān﴾" is in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ) and praise, meaning: "By this distinct Book is intended a Qur'an whose attributes are such and such." It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

The sixth is His saying "﴿ʿarabiyyan﴾." The meaning is that this Qur'an was revealed only in the language of the Arabs. This is confirmed by His saying, exalted is He: "﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people﴾ [Ibrahim: 4]."

The seventh is His saying, exalted is He, "﴿for a people who know﴾." The meaning is: We made it Arabic because We sent it down to an Arab people, so We made it in the language of the Arabs so that they might understand its intended meaning. If it is asked: "What does His saying '﴿for a people who know﴾' relate to?" We reply: It may relate to "tanzīl" or to "fuṣṣilat," meaning: "a revelation from God for their sake," or "its verses have been made distinct for their sake." The better view is that it is a qualifier, like what comes before it and after it, meaning: "an Arabic Qur'an belonging to an Arab people," so that the relative clauses (ṣilāt) and the adjectives (ṣifāt) are not distinguished from one another.

The eighth and ninth: His saying "﴿a bearer of good news and a warner﴾." That is, a bearer of good news to the obedient with reward, and a warner to the wrongdoers with punishment. The truth is that the Qur'an is good news and warning, but the name of the agent was applied to it to draw attention to its being perfect in this attribute, just as one says "a poem that is poetic" (shiʿr shāʿir) and "a speech that is speaking" (kalām qāʾil).

The tenth attribute is that they turn away from it, do not listen, and do not pay attention to it. These are the ten attributes with which God described the Qur'an. Several questions branch out from these:

First question: Those who hold that the Qur'an is created argued from this verse in several ways.

The first: He described the Qur'an as being a "tanzīl" and "munazzal," and "munazzal" and "tanzīl" imply a transformation from one state to another. Therefore it must be created.

The second: "Tanzīl" is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and by the agreement of the grammarians, the verbal noun is the absolute object (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq).

The third: The meaning of "Kitāb" is either the act of writing, which is the absolute object, or the written thing, which is the object.

The fourth: His saying "﴿fuṣṣilat﴾" indicates that someone acts upon it by way of separating and distinguishing, and that does not befit the Eternal.

The fifth: It was called "Qur'ān" only because some of its parts were joined with others, and this indicates that it is an object made by a maker and a thing produced by one who produces.

The sixth: Describing it as "ʿarabiyyan." This attribution is valid only because these words entered upon these meanings according to the convention and terminology of the Arabs, and what is made by someone's making and someone's action must be originated and created.

The answer: All these points you have mentioned pertain to languages, letters and words, and these we also consider originated and created. What we claim to be eternal is something else apart from these words. And God knows best.

Second question: Most of the theologians (mutakallimūn) hold that it is obligatory for the responsible person to interpret the words of the Qur'an according to the meanings for which they were laid down in the Arabic language. As for carrying them to other meanings not by this method, that is certainly invalid. This is like the interpretations mentioned by the people of the esoteric (ahl al-bāṭin): sometimes they take the letters according to the reckoning of abjad (ḥisāb al-jummal), and sometimes they take each letter to refer to something else. The Sufis have many methods in this domain, and they call it "the science of unveiling" (ʿilm al-mukāshafah). What proves the invalidity of all those interpretations is His saying "﴿Qur'ān ʿarabiyyan﴾." He called it "ʿarabiyyan" only because it indicates these specific meanings by the convention and terminology of the Arabs. This indicates that the signification of these words was achieved only through those specific meanings, and that whatever is other than that is invalid.

Third question: Some people held that foreign languages occur in the Qur'an, such as His saying "﴿istabraq﴾" [al-Kahf: 31] and "﴿sijjīl﴾" [Hud: 82], which are Persian; and His saying "mishkāh" [al-Nur: 35], which is from the language of Abyssinia; and His saying "qisṭās" [al-Isra': 35], which is from the language of the Romans. What proves the invalidity of this view is His saying "﴿Qur'ān ʿarabiyyan﴾" and His saying "﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people﴾" [Ibrahim: 4].

Fourth question: The Mu'tazilah said that the terms "īmān" (faith), "kufr" (disbelief), "ṣalāh" (prayer), "zakāh" (almsgiving), "ṣawm" (fasting) and "ḥajj" (pilgrimage) are legal terms (alfāẓ sharʿiyyah), not linguistic ones. The meaning is that the Law transferred these words from their original linguistic referents to other referents. In our view, this is false. The Law has no power over these words to move them from their referents except in one respect: it restricted these names to one particular type of their referents. For example, "īmān" linguistically means assent (taṣdīq), and the Law restricted it to a specific kind of assent. "Ṣalāh" linguistically means supplication (duʿāʾ), and the Law restricted it to a specific kind of supplication. The same applies to the rest. Our proof of the soundness of our position is His saying "﴿Qur'ān ʿarabiyyan﴾" and His saying "﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people﴾."

* * *

Fifth question: God described the Qur'an as being "ʿarabiyyan" in the context of praise and glorification, and this aim is not achieved unless it is established that the language of the Arabs is the best of languages.

Know that this aim is achieved only if we fix the divisions of the excellences of languages by a known criterion, and then show that those divisions are present in it and not in anything else. So we say: Undoubtedly speech is composed of single words, and words are composed of letters. A word has a matter, which is the letters, and it has a form, which is that specific shape obtained through composition. This excellence is obtained either according to its matter or according to its form. As for what is according to its matter, it is the individual letters. Know that letters are of two kinds: some are clearly articulated in their points of articulation (makhārij) and clearly distinct in their boundaries, and some are obscure in their points of articulation and confused in their boundaries. All the letters of Arabic are clearly articulated and clearly distinct in their boundaries, and none of them is confused with another.

As for the letters used in other languages, they are not like this. Rather, a letter may occur in them that is confused with another, and that harms the completeness of eloquence (faṣāḥah). Also, the vowels used in the whole of the Arabic language are clear and manifest vowels, namely the accusative (naṣb), nominative (rafʿ) and genitive (jarr). Each of these three is distinguished from the others with a clear and manifest distinction. As for the ishmām and the rawm (partial vowel-coloring techniques), their occurrence is rare in Arabic dialects, and that too belongs to the category of things that produce eloquence.

As for the words that arise from composition, they are of several kinds:

The first: Letters are of two kinds: those whose points of articulation are close and those whose points of articulation are far apart. Also, letters are of two kinds: some are hard (ṣulbah) and some are soft (raxwah). From this division there arise four categories: hard and close, soft and close, hard and distant, soft and distant. When two hard letters with close points of articulation follow one another in a word, pronouncing it becomes difficult, because the closeness of the point of articulation makes its pronunciation like what happens when a person is shackled and then walks. And because of the hardness of those letters, strong and laborious actions converge on one point of articulation, and the succession of laborious actions causes weakness and exhaustion. Such a composition is rare in the Arabic language.

The second: The nature of some letters is sweeter and more pleasant to the hearing, and any word in which a letter of this nature occurs is more pleasant to hear.

Third: the metre (wazn). We say that a word is either biliteral, triliteral or quadriliteral, and the most balanced of these is the triliteral. This is because sound is only produced through movement, and movement must have a beginning, a middle and an end. These are three stages, so a word must contain these three stages in order to be complete. The biliteral is deficient, and the quadriliteral is excessive. What predominates in the speech of the Arabs are the triliterals. Thus, by what we have mentioned, the classification of the families of languages is established. Induction (istiqra') indicates that the language of the Arabs is characterised by this, whereas the other languages are not like this. And God knows best.
