Instead He said: I created these heavy mountains above the earth, so that a person may see with his own eye that the earth and the mountains are weights upon weights, and all of them need something that holds and preserves them. And there is no such holder and manager except God, glorified and exalted.

The second kind of what God, the Exalted, informed about in this verse is His words: ﴿and blessed it﴾. Blessing (barakah) is abundance of good, and the goods that come from the earth are more than can be encompassed by explanation and exposition. We have mentioned them in detail in Surat al-Baqarah. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: he means splitting the rivers, creating the mountains, creating the trees and fruits, creating the kinds of animals, and everything they need of goods.

The third kind is His words: ﴿and measured in it its sustenance﴾. On this there are several views:

The first: the meaning is that He measured in it the sustenance of its people, their livelihoods, and what sets them right. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: He measured the sustenance of bodies before He created the bodies.

The second view: Mujahid said: ﴿and measured in it its sustenance﴾ means from the rain. According to this view, the sustenance belongs to the earth, not to the inhabitants, and the meaning is that God measured for each land its share of rain.

The third view: the intended meaning of attributing the sustenance to the earth is that it is generated from that earth and occurs in it. The grammarians said that a minimal cause is enough for the goodness of an attribution: a thing is sometimes attributed to its agent, and sometimes to its locus. So His words ﴿and measured in it its sustenance﴾ mean: He measured the sustenances whose occurrence is specific to it. This is because God made each town a source of another kind of desired things, so that the people of this town need the things generated in that town, and vice versa. This meaning became a cause for people's desire for trade and the acquisition of wealth.

I have seen some who used to say that the craft of farming and tilling is the most blessed of crafts and trades, because God placed the provisions and sustenance in the earth. He said: ﴿and measured in it its sustenance﴾, and when the sustenance is placed in the earth, seeking it from the earth becomes necessary.

When God, glorified be He, mentioned these three kinds of arrangement, He said after them: ﴿in four days, equally for those who ask﴾. Here there are questions:

The first question: He mentioned that He created the earth in two days, and mentioned that He set right these three kinds in four other days, and mentioned that He created the heavens in two days. The total would then be eight days. But in other verses He mentioned that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, so a contradiction arises.

Know that the scholars answered this by saying: what is meant by His words ﴿and measured in it its sustenance in four days﴾ is together with the first two days. This is like the saying of someone: "I traveled from Basra to Baghdad in ten days, and I traveled to Kufa in fifteen days," meaning both journeys together. And a man says to another: "I gave you a thousand in a month, and thousands in two months," so the thousand is included in the thousands and the month in the two months.

The second question: since He mentioned that He created the earth in two days, if He had mentioned that He created these three remaining kinds in two other days, that would have been further from doubt and further from error. Why did He leave this explicit statement and mention that general speech?

[Page 90]

The answer: His words ﴿in four days, equally for those who ask﴾ carry a benefit that would not be there if He had said: "I created these three in two days." That is because if He had said: "I created these things in two days," while the two days were not entirely occupied by that work, but when He mentioned the creation of the earth and the creation of these things, and then said after it ﴿in four days, equally for those who ask﴾, this indicates that these four days became entirely occupied with those works, without any excess or deficiency.

The third question: how are the readings of His word (sawā'an, "equally")? The answer: the author of al-Kashshaf said: it is read (sawā'an) with the three vowels: the genitive (jarr) as a qualifier, the accusative (nasb) as a verbal noun (maṣdar), as in "it became equal" (istawat sawā'an), and the nominative (raf') as in "it is equal" (hiya sawā'un).

The fourth question: what is meant by those four days being equal? We say: days may be of equal lengths, as the days found at the places on the equator, and they may be of different lengths, as the days found in the rest of the places. So He, the Exalted, made clear that those four days were equal, not different.

The fifth question: to what does His words (lil-sā'ilīn, "for those who ask") relate?

The answer has two aspects:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: His words ﴿in four days﴾ mean "in the completion of four days." Knowing this, the meaning is: ﴿and measured in it its sustenance﴾ in the completion of four days, for the sake of those who ask, that is, those who seek sustenance and are in need of it.

The second: it relates to an omitted element. The meaning is as if it were said: this specification and explanation are for the sake of one who asked how much the earth was created and what is in it. When God, the Exalted, explained how the earth and what is in it were created, He followed it with how the heavens were created, and said: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven, and it was smoke.﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: His words ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ come from the saying of people: "he turned (istawā) to such-and-such a place," when he directed himself to it with a direction in which he does not turn aside to any other work. It is from istiwā' (evenness), which is the opposite of crookedness. Its parallel is the saying: "he went straight toward it" (istaqāma ilayhi) and "he extended toward it" (imtadda ilayhi). From it is His word: ﴿So go straight to Him﴾ [Fussilat: 6]. The meaning is: then the caller of wisdom summoned Him to create the heaven after creating the earth and what is in it, without any diversion that would turn Him away from it.

The second investigation: the author of "al-Athar" (the book of narrations) mentioned that God's Throne was upon the water before the creation of the heavens and the earth. God then caused the water to become heated, and foam and smoke rose from it. As for the foam, it remained on the surface of the water, and God created dryness from it and brought the earth into being from it. As for the smoke, it rose and ascended, and God created the heavens from it.

Know that this story is not found in the Qur'an. If a sound proof indicates it, it is accepted; otherwise it is not. This story is mentioned at the beginning of the book that the Jews claim is the Torah, and in it God created the sky from dark particles. This is what is rational, because we have demonstrated in the rational sciences (al-ma'qulat) that darkness is not an existential quality (kayfiyyah wujudiyyah), by the evidence that if a person sits in the light of a lamp and another person sits in darkness, the one sitting in the light does not see the place of the one sitting in darkness, and sees that air as dark.

As for the one who sat in darkness, he sees the one who was sitting in the light, and sees that air as luminous. Had darkness been a quality subsisting in the air, the states would not have differed according to the differing states of the observers. Thus it is established that darkness is an expression for the absence of light. Then, when God assembled it and made it into heavens, stars, a sun and a moon, and caused the quality of light to occur in them, they then became illuminated. It is thus established that those particles, when God intended to create from them the heavens, the sun
Page 91
and the moon, were dark, and so it is correct to call them "smoke," for smoke has no meaning except particles scattered, not continuous, lacking light. This is what came to mind regarding the explanation of the smoke, and God knows best the reality of the matter.

The third investigation: His saying, ﴿Then He istawa toward the heaven, and it was smoke﴾, indicates that the creation of the heaven occurred after the creation of the earth, and His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30], indicates that the creation of the earth occurred after the creation of the heaven. That entails contradiction. The scholars differed on this question, and the well-known answer is to say: He, the Exalted, created the earth in two days first, then after it created the heaven, and then after the creation of the heaven He spread out the earth. By this way the contradiction disappears.

Know that this answer is problematic in my view for several reasons:

The first: He, the Exalted, made clear that He created the earth in two days, then on the third day ﴿He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance﴾. These conditions cannot be brought into existence except after the earth had become spread out (madhuwwah), because the creation of mountains in it is not possible except after the earth had become spread out and flat. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and blessed in it﴾ is explained as the creation of trees, plants and animals in it, and that is not possible except after it became flattened. Then He, the Exalted, said after that, ﴿Then He istawa toward the heaven﴾. This requires that He, the Exalted, created the heaven after the creation of the earth and after making it spread out. And then the aforementioned question returns.

The second: Geometric proofs have indicated that the earth is a sphere. So either we say that it was a sphere at its first origination and now it remains a sphere, in which case it has been spread out since it was created; or we say that it was not a sphere and then was made into a sphere, in which case it must be said that it was spread out before that and then this quality was removed from it, and that is false.

The third: The earth is a body of utmost greatness, and a body of that kind is spread out from the first moment of its entry into existence, so the claim that it was not spread out and then became spread out is a false claim. What has come in the books of history is that the earth was created at the place of the rock in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). That is a problematic statement, because if the meaning is that it was created in that place with all its greatness, this is a claim of the interpenetration of dense bodies, which is impossible.

And if the meaning is that He first created small particles in that place and then created the rest of its parts, which were added to those particles created first, then this would be an acknowledgment that the creation of the earth occurred later than the creation of the heaven.

The fourth: Since the creation of the essence of the earth occurred in two days, and the creation of all other things existing in the earth occurred in two other days, and the creation of the heavens occurred in two other days, the total of that is six days. If the spreading of the earth occurs after that, then this spreading occurs at a time after the six days, and then the creation of the heavens and earth occurs over more than six days, and that is false.

The fifth: There is no dispute that His saying, the Exalted, after this verse, ﴿Then He istawa toward the heaven, and it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: Come both, willingly or unwillingly﴾ is a metaphor (kinayah) for bringing the heaven and the earth into existence. So if the bringing into existence of the heaven preceded the bringing into existence of the earth, His saying ﴿Come willingly or unwillingly﴾ would require bringing into existence what already exists, and that is impossible and false.

This is the complete discussion of this well-known answer. Al-Wahidi, in "al-Basit," transmitted from Muqatil that he said: God created the heavens before the earth, and the interpretation of His saying ﴿Then He istawa toward the heaven﴾ is: then He had istawa toward the heaven, and it was smoke, and said to it before He created the earth. So He concealed within it "had," as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They said: If he steals, a brother of his stole before﴾ [Yusuf: 77], meaning "if he has stolen," and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And how many a town We destroyed, and Our might came to it﴾ [al-A'raf: 4], meaning "it had come to it."

This is what al-Wahidi transmitted, and it is weak in my view, because the construction of the sentence becomes "then He had istawa toward the heaven," and this is a combining of opposites, because the word "then" (thumma) requires delay, and the word "had" (kana) requires priority, and combining them yields contradiction. That is evidence that it was not possible to take it according to its apparent meaning. We have shown that His saying ﴿Come willingly or unwillingly﴾ occurred before their existence, and if that is so, it is impossible to interpret His saying "come" as a command and an obligation, so it must be interpreted as we have mentioned.

Questions remain regarding the wording of the verse:

First question: What is the benefit in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: Come both, willingly or unwillingly﴾? Answer: The purpose of it is to manifest the perfection of power, and the sense is: "Come, whether you wish it or not," as a mighty one says to those under his hand: "You will do this whether you want to or not, and you will do it willingly or unwillingly." Their two words are in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal), meaning "willing" or "unwilling." (They said: "We came willingly.") It is said also that He, the Exalted, mentioned the heaven and the earth, then mentioned willingness and unwillingness, so willingness must be ascribed to the heaven and unwillingness to the earth, by singling out the heaven for willingness, for several reasons:

One of them: the heaven in the continuity of its motion follows one course without variation, resembling an obedient living being to God, the Exalted, unlike the earth, which is varied in its states, sometimes at rest and at other times in agitated motions.

The second: what exists in the heaven has nothing but obedience, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Nahl: 50]. As for the people of the earth, the matter is not so with regard to them.

The third: the heaven is described with perfection of condition in all matters. They said: it is the finest of colors, which is luminous; its shapes are the finest shapes, which is round; its place is the finest of places, which is the high atmosphere; its bodies are the finest of bodies, which are the sparkling stars. Unlike the earth, which is the place of darkness, density, variation of states, and change of essences and attributes.

Therefore the expression of the heaven's coming into being is in terms of willingness, and the expression of the earth's coming into being is in terms of unwillingness. And since the basis of the earth's creation is unwillingness, its people are forever described by what entails unwillingness, distress, subjugation and compulsion.

Second question: What is meant by His saying "Come" and by their saying "We came"? Answer: What is meant is "Come into existence and occurrence," and it is like His saying ﴿Be, and it is﴾. It is also said: the meaning is "Come in the form and attribute in which you ought to come," that is, the earth spread out as a resting place and cradle, and the heaven raised as a roof over them. And the meaning of "coming" is attainment and occurrence in accordance with the will, as you say: "his deed came pleasing" and "came accepted." It is also permissible that the meaning be: let each of you come to the other with the coming that wisdom and governance require, of the earth being a resting place for the heaven and the heaven being a roof for the earth.

Third question: Why was it not said "obedient" (ta'i'in) in the masculine according to the wording, or "obedient" (ta'i'at) in the feminine according to the meaning, since they are heavens and earths? Answer: When they were made addressees and respondents, and were charged with willingness and unwillingness, it was said "ta'i'in" in place of "ta'i'at," like His saying "prostrating" (sajidin) [al-Hijr: 29]. Some of them used this as evidence that the heavens are living beings, saying: the earth within the heavens is smaller than a tiny atom within a great mountain, so for this reason the word denoting reason and life became dominant. However, this view is false, by the consensus of the theologians on its corruption.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾. The decreeing (qada') of a thing is only its completion and finishing with it. The pronoun in His saying ﴿fa-qadahunna﴾ may refer to the heavens according to the meaning, as in "obedient" and similar, ﴿the trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7]. It may also be an ambiguous pronoun explained by "seven heavens." The difference between the two accusatives is that one is a circumstantial state (hal) and the second is a specification (tamyiz).

If it is said: "day" is an expression for day and night, and that occurs only through the rising and setting of the sun, and before the existence of the heavens, sun and moon, how can the existence of a day be conceived?

Know that when the Exalted commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) in the first verse to say: ﴿I am only a human being like you. It is revealed to me that your God is one God. So go straight to Him and seek His forgiveness﴾, He followed it with what indicates that it is not permissible to affirm a partnership between Him, the Exalted, and these idols in divinity and worship. This is done by showing His perfect power and wisdom in creating the heavens and the earth in a short period. How, then, is it permissible to make the base idols partners with Him in divinity and worship, when He is described by this attribute? This is the explanation of the arrangement (nazm, the coherence of the verses). In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir recited: ﴿أيِنَّكم لَتَكْفُرُونَ﴾ (ayinnakum, with a hamza, then a light, unvoweled yā' without a madd). As for Nafi' in the narration of Qalun and Abu 'Amr, they follow this form, except that both of them prolong (the vowel). The rest read two hamzas without a madd.

The second issue: The Exalted's words (أئنكم) are an interrogative with the meaning of denunciation. He mentioned two denounced things about them:

One of them is disbelief in God, which is His words: ﴿you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days﴾. The second is ascribing partners and rivals to Him. The disbelief mentioned first must be different from ascribing rivals to Him, because coordinating one of them with the other necessitates difference. The most apparent view is that what is meant by their disbelief has several aspects:

The first: their saying that God, the Exalted, has no power to resurrect the dead. Since they disputed the existence of this power, they disbelieved in God.

The second: they used to dispute the validity of religious obligation (taklif) and the sending of prophets. All of this is a discrediting of the attributes that are required for divinity, and it is disbelief in God.

The third: they used to attribute children to Him, and this too is a discrediting of divinity, which entails disbelief in God. The summary is that they disbelieved in God because of their saying these things, and they also affirmed rivals to God because of their saying that those idols are divine. The Exalted argued against the falsity of their view by causation, saying: How is it permissible to disbelieve in God, and how is it permissible to make these base idols rivals to God, the Exalted, when He is the One who created the earth in two days, completed the rest of its interests in two other days, and created all the heavens in two other days?

Whoever is able to create these great things, how is it conceivable to disbelieve in Him, or to deny His power to resurrect and gather? And how is it conceivable to deny His power over obligation and over the sending of prophets? And how is it conceivable to make these base idols rivals to Him in worship and divinity?

If it is said: whoever argues from one thing to establish another, that thing he argues from must be accepted by the opponent so that the argument is valid. And God's creating the earth in two days is a matter that cannot be established by pure reason; it can only be established by revelation (sam') and the revelation of the prophets.

The disbelievers disputed revelation and prophethood, so it is not conceivable to present this premise to them. And if presenting this premise to them is impossible, then arguing with it against the falsity of their positions is also impossible.

We say: establishing that the heavens and the earth are created through an act is possible. When this is established, it is possible to argue from it to the existence of the God who is all-powerful, dominant, and great. Then it is said to the disbelievers: how is it conceivable to equate the God described by this overpowering power with an idol, which is an inert object that neither harms nor benefits, in worship and divinity?

It remains to be said: then, in that case, the argument from God's creating the earth in two days has no effect. We say: this too has an effect in this matter, because the beginning of the Torah contains this meaning, and so it was extremely well known among the People of the Book. The Meccan disbelievers believed of the People of the Book that they were the people of knowledge and realities. It is apparent that they had heard these meanings from the People of the Book and believed them to be true. When this is the case, it is good to say to them: the God described as having power to create great things in this short period, how is it fitting for reason to make a carpentered wood and a carved stone a partner to Him in worship and divinity? From what we have established, it is clear that this argument is strong and good.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and blessed in it﴾ is explained as the creation of trees, plants and animals in it, and that is not possible except after it became flattened. And then the aforementioned question returns.

The second: Geometric proofs have indicated that the earth is a sphere. So either we say that it was a sphere at its first origination and now it remains a sphere, in which case it has been spread out since it was created; or we say that it was not a sphere and then was made into a sphere, in which case it must be said that it was spread out before that and then this quality was removed from it, and that is false.

The third: The earth is a body of utmost greatness, and a body of that kind is spread out from the first moment of its entry into existence, so the claim that it was not spread out and then became spread out is a false claim. What has come in the books of history is that the earth was created at the place of the rock in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). That is a problematic statement, because if the meaning is that it was created in that place with all its greatness, this is a claim of the interpenetration of dense bodies, which is impossible.

And if the meaning is that He first created small particles in that place and then created the rest of its parts, which were added to those particles created first, then this would be an acknowledgment that the creation of the earth occurred later than the creation of the heaven.

The fourth: Since the creation of the essence of the earth occurred in two days, and the creation of all other things existing in the earth occurred in two other days, and the creation of the heavens occurred in two other days, the total of that is six days. If the spreading of the earth occurs after that, then this spreading occurs at a time after the six days, and then the creation of the heavens and earth occurs over more than six days, and that is false.

The fifth: There is no dispute that His saying, the Exalted, after this verse, ﴿Then He istawa toward the heaven, and it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: Come both, willingly or unwillingly﴾ is a metaphor (kinayah) for bringing the heaven and the earth into existence. So if the bringing into existence of the heaven preceded the bringing into existence of the earth, His saying ﴿Come willingly or unwillingly﴾ would require bringing into existence what already exists, and that is impossible and false.

This is the complete discussion of this well-known answer. Al-Wahidi, in "al-Basit," transmitted from Muqatil that he said: God created the heavens before the earth, and the interpretation of His saying ﴿Then He istawa toward the heaven﴾ is: then He had istawa toward the heaven, and it was smoke, and said to it before He created the earth. So He concealed within it "had," as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They said: If he steals, a brother of his stole before﴾ [Yusuf: 77], meaning "if he has stolen," and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And how many a town We destroyed, and Our might came to it﴾ [al-A'raf: 4], meaning "it had come to it."

This is what al-Wahidi transmitted, and it is weak in my view, because the construction of the sentence becomes "then He had istawa toward the heaven," and this is a combining of opposites, because the word "then" (thumma) requires delay, and the word "had" (kana) requires priority, and combining them yields contradiction. That is evidence that it was not possible to take it according to its apparent meaning. We have shown that His saying ﴿Come willingly or unwillingly﴾ occurred before their existence, and if that is so, it is impossible to interpret His saying "come" as a command and an obligation, so it must be interpreted as we have mentioned.

Questions remain regarding the wording of the verse:

First question: What is the benefit in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: Come both, willingly or unwillingly﴾? Answer: The purpose of it is to manifest the perfection of power, and the sense is: "Come, whether you wish it or not," as a mighty one says to those under his hand: "You will do this whether you want to or not, and you will do it willingly or unwillingly." Their two words are in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal), meaning "willing" or "unwilling." (They said: "We came willingly.") It is said also that He, the Exalted, mentioned the heaven and the earth, then mentioned willingness and unwillingness, so willingness must be ascribed to the heaven and unwillingness to the earth, by singling out the heaven for willingness, for several reasons:

One of them: the heaven in the continuity of its motion follows one course without variation, resembling an obedient living being to God, the Exalted, unlike the earth, which is varied in its states, sometimes at rest and at other times in agitated motions.

The second: what exists in the heaven has nothing but obedience, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Nahl: 50]. As for the people of the earth, the matter is not so with regard to them.

The third: the heaven is described with perfection of condition in all matters. They said: it is the finest of colors, which is luminous; its shapes are the finest shapes, which is round; its place is the finest of places, which is the high atmosphere; its bodies are the finest of bodies, which are the sparkling stars. Unlike the earth, which is the place of darkness, density, variation of states, and change of essences and attributes.

Therefore the expression of the heaven's coming into being is in terms of willingness, and the expression of the earth's coming into being is in terms of unwillingness. And since the basis of the earth's creation is unwillingness, its people are forever described by what entails unwillingness, distress, subjugation and compulsion.

Second question: What is meant by His saying "Come" and by their saying "We came"? Answer: What is meant is "Come into existence and occurrence," and it is like His saying ﴿Be, and it is﴾. It is also said: the meaning is "Come in the form and attribute in which you ought to come," that is, the earth spread out as a resting place and cradle, and the heaven raised as a roof over them. And the meaning of "coming" is attainment and occurrence in accordance with the will, as you say: "his deed came pleasing" and "came accepted." It is also permissible that the meaning be: let each of you come to the other with the coming that wisdom and governance require, of the earth being a resting place for the heaven and the heaven being a roof for the earth.

Third question: Why was it not said "obedient" (ta'i'in) in the masculine according to the wording, or "obedient" (ta'i'at) in the feminine according to the meaning, since they are heavens and earths? Answer: When they were made addressees and respondents, and were charged with willingness and unwillingness, it was said "ta'i'in" in place of "ta'i'at," like His saying "prostrating" (sajidin) [al-Hijr: 29]. Some of them used this as evidence that the heavens are living beings, saying: the earth within the heavens is smaller than a tiny atom within a great mountain, so for this reason the word denoting reason and life became dominant. However, this view is false, by the consensus of the theologians on its corruption.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾. The decreeing (qada') of a thing is only its completion and finishing with it. The pronoun in His saying ﴿fa-qadahunna﴾ may refer to the heavens according to the meaning, as in "obedient" and similar, ﴿the trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7]. It may also be an ambiguous pronoun explained by "seven heavens." The difference between the two accusatives is that one is a circumstantial state (hal) and the second is a specification (tamyiz).

The people of transmitted reports (ahl al-athar) mentioned that God created the earth on Sunday and Monday, and created what is in the rest of the earth on Tuesday and Wednesday, and created the heavens and what is in them on Thursday and Friday, and He finished in the last hour of Friday, creating Adam in it, and that is the hour in which the Resurrection will occur. If it is said: "day" is an expression for day and night, and that occurs only through the rising and setting of the sun, and before the existence of the heavens, sun and moon, how can the existence of a day be conceived?

The Exalted said: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days, and set up rivals to Him? Know that when the Exalted commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) in the first verse to say: ﴿I am only a human being like you. It is revealed to me that your God is one God. So go straight to Him and seek His forgiveness﴾, He followed it with what indicates that it is not permissible to affirm a partnership between Him, the Exalted, and these idols in divinity and worship. This is done by showing His perfect power and wisdom in creating the heavens and the earth in a short period. How, then, is it permissible to make the base idols partners with Him in divinity and worship, when He is described by this attribute? This is the explanation of the arrangement (nazm, the coherence of the verses). In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir recited: ﴿أيِنَّكم لَتَكْفُرُونَ﴾ (ayinnakum, with a hamza, then a light, unvoweled yā' without a madd). As for Nafi' in the narration of Qalun and Abu 'Amr, they follow this form, except that both of them prolong (the vowel). The rest read two hamzas without a madd.

The second issue: The Exalted's words (أئنكم) are an interrogative with the meaning of denunciation. He mentioned two denounced things about them:

One of them is disbelief in God, which is His words: ﴿you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days﴾. The second is ascribing partners and rivals to Him. The disbelief mentioned first must be different from ascribing rivals to Him, because coordinating one of them with the other necessitates difference. The most apparent view is that what is meant by their disbelief has several aspects:

The first: their saying that God, the Exalted, has no power to resurrect the dead. Since they disputed the existence of this power, they disbelieved in God.

The second: they used to dispute the validity of religious obligation (taklif) and the sending of prophets. All of this is a discrediting of the attributes that are required for divinity, and it is disbelief in God.

The third: they used to attribute children to Him, and this too is a discrediting of divinity, which entails disbelief in God. The summary is that they disbelieved in God because of their saying these things, and they also affirmed rivals to God because of their saying that those idols are divine. The Exalted argued against the falsity of their view by causation, saying: How is it permissible to disbelieve in God, and how is it permissible to make these base idols rivals to God, the Exalted, when He is the One who created the earth in two days, completed the rest of its interests in two other days, and created all the heavens in two other days?

Whoever is able to create these great things, how is it conceivable to disbelieve in Him, or to deny His power to resurrect and gather? And how is it conceivable to deny His power over obligation and over the sending of prophets? And how is it conceivable to make these base idols rivals to Him in worship and divinity?

If it is said: whoever argues from one thing to establish another, that thing he argues from must be accepted by the opponent so that the argument is valid. And God's creating the earth in two days is a matter that cannot be established by pure reason; it can only be established by revelation (sam') and the revelation of the prophets.

The disbelievers disputed revelation and prophethood, so it is not conceivable to present this premise to them. And if presenting this premise to them is impossible, then arguing with it against the falsity of their positions is also impossible.

We say: establishing that the heavens and the earth are created through an act is possible. When this is established, it is possible to argue from it to the existence of the God who is all-powerful, dominant, and great. Then it is said to the disbelievers: how is it conceivable to equate the God described by this overpowering power with an idol, which is an inert object that neither harms nor benefits, in worship and divinity?

It remains to be said: then, in that case, the argument from God's creating the earth in two days has no effect. We say: this too has an effect in this matter, because the beginning of the Torah contains this meaning, and so it was extremely well known among the People of the Book. The Meccan disbelievers believed of the People of the Book that they were the people of knowledge and realities. It is apparent that they had heard these meanings from the People of the Book and believed them to be true. When this is the case, it is good to say to them: the God described as having power to create great things in this short period, how is it fitting for reason to make a carpentered wood and a carved stone a partner to Him in worship and divinity? From what we have established, it is clear that this argument is strong and good.

As for the Exalted's words: ﴿That is the Lord of the worlds﴾, that is: that existent One whose attribute and power you have known, who created the earth in two days, is the Lord of the worlds, their Creator and Originator. So how have you affirmed for Him rivals made of wood and stone?

Then, when He informed about His being the Creator of the earth in two days, He informed that after that He brought three kinds of wondrous craftsmanship and marvelous action. The first is His words: ﴿And He placed firm mountains upon it, above it﴾, and what is meant by them is the mountains. The explanation of their being ﴿firm﴾ has already been given in Surat al-Nahl.

If it is asked: what is the point of His words ﴿above it﴾? Why did He not limit Himself to His words ﴿And He placed firm mountains upon it﴾, as in His words: ﴿And We placed upon it firm towering mountains﴾ [al-Mursalat: 27] and ﴿And We placed upon the earth firm mountains﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3]?

We say: because if He had placed mountains upon it from beneath it, that would have suggested that those lower pillars were what held this heavy earth from falling. Instead He said: I created these heavy mountains above the earth, so that a person may see with his own eye that the earth and the mountains are weights upon weights, and all of them need something that holds and preserves them. And there is no such holder and manager except God, glorified and exalted.

The second kind of what God, the Exalted, informed about in this verse is His words: ﴿and blessed it﴾. Blessing (barakah) is abundance of good, and the goods that come from the earth are more than can be encompassed by explanation and exposition. We have mentioned them in detail in Surat al-Baqarah. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: he means splitting the rivers, creating the mountains, creating the trees and fruits, creating the kinds of animals, and everything they need of goods.

The third kind is His words: ﴿and measured in it its sustenance﴾. On this there are several views:

The first: the meaning is that He measured in it the sustenance of its people, their livelihoods, and what sets them right. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: He measured the sustenance of bodies before He created the bodies.

The second view: Mujahid said: ﴿and measured in it its sustenance﴾ means from the rain. According to this view, the sustenance belongs to the earth, not to the inhabitants, and the meaning is that God measured for each land its share of rain.

The third view: the intended meaning of attributing the sustenance to the earth is that it is generated from that earth and occurs in it. The grammarians said that a minimal cause is enough for the goodness of an attribution: a thing is sometimes attributed to its agent, and sometimes to its locus. So His words ﴿and measured in it its sustenance﴾ mean: He measured the sustenances whose occurrence is specific to it. This is because God made each town a source of another kind of desired things, so that the people of this town need the things generated in that town, and vice versa. This meaning became a cause for people's desire for trade and the acquisition of wealth.

I have seen some who used to say that the craft of farming and tilling is the most blessed of crafts and trades, because God placed the provisions and sustenance in the earth. He said: ﴿and measured in it its sustenance﴾, and when the sustenance is placed in the earth, seeking it from the earth becomes necessary.

When God, glorified be He, mentioned these three kinds of arrangement, He said after them: ﴿in four days, equally for those who ask﴾. Here there are questions:

The first question: He mentioned that He created the earth in two days, and mentioned that He set right these three kinds in four other days, and mentioned that He created the heavens in two days. The total would then be eight days. But in other verses He mentioned that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, so a contradiction arises.

Know that the scholars answered this by saying: what is meant by His words ﴿and measured in it its sustenance in four days﴾ is together with the first two days. This is like the saying of someone: "I traveled from Basra to Baghdad in ten days, and I traveled to Kufa in fifteen days," meaning both journeys together. And a man says to another: "I gave you a thousand in a month, and thousands in two months," so the thousand is included in the thousands and the month in the two months.

The second question: since He mentioned that He created the earth in two days, if He had mentioned that He created these three remaining kinds in two other days, that would have been further from doubt and further from error. Why did He leave this explicit statement and mention that general speech?

[Page 90]

The answer: His words ﴿in four days, equally for those who ask﴾ carry a benefit that would not be there if He had said: "I created these three in two days." That is because if He had said: "I created these things in two days," while the two days were not entirely occupied by that work, but when He mentioned the creation of the earth and the creation of these things, and then said after it ﴿in four days, equally for those who ask﴾, this indicates that these four days became entirely occupied with those works, without any excess or deficiency.

The third question: how are the readings of His word (sawā'an, "equally")? The answer: the author of al-Kashshaf said: it is read (sawā'an) with the three vowels: the genitive (jarr) as a qualifier, the accusative (nasb) as a verbal noun (maṣdar), as in "it became equal" (istawat sawā'an), and the nominative (raf') as in "it is equal" (hiya sawā'un).

The fourth question: what is meant by those four days being equal? We say: days may be of equal lengths, as the days found at the places on the equator, and they may be of different lengths, as the days found in the rest of the places. So He, the Exalted, made clear that those four days were equal, not different.

The fifth question: to what does His words (lil-sā'ilīn, "for those who ask") relate?

The answer has two aspects:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: His words ﴿in four days﴾ mean "in the completion of four days." Knowing this, the meaning is: ﴿and measured in it its sustenance﴾ in the completion of four days, for the sake of those who ask, that is, those who seek sustenance and are in need of it.

The second: it relates to an omitted element. The meaning is as if it were said: this specification and explanation are for the sake of one who asked how much the earth was created and what is in it. When God, the Exalted, explained how the earth and what is in it were created, He followed it with how the heavens were created, and said: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven, and it was smoke.﴾ And in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: His words ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ come from the saying of people: "he turned (istawā) to such-and-such a place," when he directed himself to it with a direction in which he does not turn aside to any other work. It is from istiwā' (evenness), which is the opposite of crookedness. Its parallel is the saying: "he went straight toward it" (istaqāma ilayhi) and "he extended toward it" (imtadda ilayhi). From it is His word: ﴿So go straight to Him﴾ [Fussilat: 6]. The meaning is: then the caller of wisdom summoned Him to create the heaven after creating the earth and what is in it, without any diversion that would turn Him away from it.

The second investigation: the author of "al-Athar" (the book of narrations) mentioned that God's Throne was upon the water before the creation of the heavens and the earth. God then caused the water to become heated, and foam and smoke rose from it. As for the foam, it remained on the surface of the water, and God created dryness from it and brought the earth into being from it. As for the smoke, it rose and ascended, and God created the heavens from it.

Know that this story is not found in the Qur'an. If a sound proof indicates it, it is accepted; otherwise it is not. This story is mentioned at the beginning of the book that the Jews claim is the Torah, and in it God created the sky from dark particles. This is what is rational, because we have demonstrated in the rational sciences (al-ma'qulat) that darkness is not an existential quality (kayfiyyah wujudiyyah), by the evidence that if a person sits in the light of a lamp and another person sits in darkness, the one sitting in the light does not see the place of the one sitting in darkness, and sees that air as dark.

As for the one who sat in darkness, he sees the one who was sitting in the light, and sees that air as luminous. Had darkness been a quality subsisting in the air, the states would not have differed according to the differing states of the observers. Thus it is established that darkness is an expression for the absence of light. Then, when God assembled it and made it into heavens, stars, a sun and a moon, and caused the quality of light to occur in them, they then became illuminated. It is thus established that those particles, when God intended to create from them the heavens, the sun

and the moon, were dark, and so it is correct to call them "smoke," for smoke has no meaning except particles scattered, not continuous, lacking light. This is what came to mind regarding the explanation of the smoke, and God knows best the reality of the matter.

The third investigation: His saying, ﴿Then He istawa toward the heaven, and it was smoke﴾, indicates that the creation of the heaven occurred after the creation of the earth, and His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30], indicates that the creation of the earth occurred after the creation of the heaven. That entails contradiction. The scholars differed on this question, and the well-known answer is to say: He, the Exalted, created the earth in two days first, then after it created the heaven, and then after the creation of the heaven He spread out the earth. By this way the contradiction disappears.

Know that this answer is problematic in my view for several reasons:

The first: He, the Exalted, made clear that He created the earth in two days, then on the third day ﴿He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance﴾. These conditions cannot be brought into existence except after the earth had become spread out (madhuwwah), because the creation of mountains in it is not possible except after the earth had become spread out and flat. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and blessed in it﴾ is explained as the creation of trees, plants and animals in it, and that is not possible except after it became flattened. Then He, the Exalted, said after that, ﴿Then He istawa toward the heaven﴾. This requires that He, the Exalted, created the heaven after the creation of the earth and after making it spread out. And then the aforementioned question returns.

The second: Geometric proofs have indicated that the earth is a sphere. So either we say that it was a sphere at its first origination and now it remains a sphere, in which case it has been spread out since it was created; or we say that it was not a sphere and then was made into a sphere, in which case it must be said that it was spread out before that and then this quality was removed from it, and that is false.

The third: The earth is a body of utmost greatness, and a body of that kind is spread out from the first moment of its entry into existence, so the claim that it was not spread out and then became spread out is a false claim. What has come in the books of history is that the earth was created at the place of the rock in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). That is a problematic statement, because if the meaning is that it was created in that place with all its greatness, this is a claim of the interpenetration of dense bodies, which is impossible.

And if the meaning is that He first created small particles in that place and then created the rest of its parts, which were added to those particles created first, then this would be an acknowledgment that the creation of the earth occurred later than the creation of the heaven.

The fourth: Since the creation of the essence of the earth occurred in two days, and the creation of all other things existing in the earth occurred in two other days, and the creation of the heavens occurred in two other days, the total of that is six days. If the spreading of the earth occurs after that, then this spreading occurs at a time after the six days, and then the creation of the heavens and earth occurs over more than six days, and that is false.

The fifth: There is no dispute that His saying, the Exalted, after this verse, ﴿Then He istawa toward the heaven, and it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: Come both, willingly or unwillingly﴾ is a metaphor (kinayah) for bringing the heaven and the earth into existence. So if the bringing into existence of the heaven preceded the bringing into existence of the earth, His saying ﴿Come willingly or unwillingly﴾ would require bringing into existence what already exists, and that is impossible and false.

We have shown that His saying ﴿Come willingly or unwillingly﴾ occurred before their existence, and if that is so, it is impossible to interpret His saying "come" as a command and an obligation, so it must be interpreted as we have mentioned.

It may also be an ambiguous pronoun explained by "seven heavens." The difference between the two accusatives is that one is a circumstantial state (hal) and the second is a specification (tamyiz).

Page 93

The people of transmitted reports (ahl al-athar) mentioned that God created the earth on Sunday and Monday, and created what is in the rest of the earth on Tuesday and Wednesday, and created the heavens and what is in them on Thursday and Friday, and He finished in the last hour of Friday, creating Adam in it, and that is the hour in which the Resurrection will occur. If it is said: "day" is an expression for day and night, and that occurs only through the rising and setting of the sun, and before the existence of the heavens, sun and moon, how can the existence of a day be conceived?

We say: its meaning is that there passed of duration what, if a sphere and a sun had existed there, the measure would have been determined as one day.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He inspired in each heaven its affair.﴾ Muqatil said: He commanded in each heaven what He willed. Qatadah said: He created in them their sun, their moon and their stars. As-Suddi said: He created in each heaven that He created from the angels and what is in it of seas and mountains of hail. He said: For Allah, in each heaven there is a house (bayt) to which the angels come in pilgrimage and circumambulate it, each one of them facing the Ka'bah; and if a pebble were to fall from it, it would fall only upon the Ka'bah. The closer view is to say: it is established in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-nahw) that even the slightest connection suffices for the goodness of an idafah (genitive construction), and Allah the Exalted has a specific obligation (taklif) upon the inhabitants of each heaven.

Among the angels there is one who is standing from the beginning of the creation of the world until the Resurrection, and among them are those who are bowing and never straighten up, and among them are those who are prostrating and never raise their heads. And if that matter is specific to the inhabitants of that heaven, then that matter is specific to that heaven. And His saying the Exalted: ﴿And He inspired in each heaven its affair﴾ means: He had assigned to each heaven the affair attributed to it, like His saying: ﴿And how many a town We have destroyed, and Our punishment came upon it by night or while they were napping﴾ [al-A'raf: 4], meaning: it had already come to it.

This is what al-Wahidi transmitted, and in my view it is weak; because the sense of the speech would be: "Then He had risen to the heaven, and He had inspired," and this is a combination of two opposites, since the word thumma (then) requires delay and the word kana (was) requires precedence, so combining them yields contradiction. Its parallel is the saying of one who says: "I struck Zayd today, then I struck ʿAmr yesterday." Just as this is invalid, so is what you have mentioned. The interpretation of Allah's speech is permitted only in ways that do not lead to contradiction or incoherence in it.

The preferred view in my opinion is to say: the creation of the heavens precedes the creation of the earth. There remains the question: what is the interpretation of this verse? We say: creation (khalq) is not an expression for bringing into being and origination, rather it is an expression for determination (taqdir), and determination is the right of Allah the Exalted, namely His judgment that He will bring it into being and His decree concerning that. When this is established, we say: His saying ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾ means that He decreed its coming into being in two days, and Allah's decree that He will bring about such-and-such in such-and-such a period does not require that thing to come into being at present. So Allah the Exalted's decree concerning the coming into being of the earth in two days preceded the origination of the heaven, and it does not follow from this that the origination of the earth preceded the origination of the heaven. At that point the question is removed. This is what I have reached concerning this problematic passage.

* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So He said to it and to the earth, "Come both of you willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly."﴾

Know that the apparent meaning of this speech requires that Allah the Exalted commanded the heaven and the earth to come, and they obeyed and complied. At this point two views arise concerning the verse:

The first view: that this verse be taken according to its apparent meaning. We say: Allah the Exalted commanded them both to come, and they obeyed Him. Those who hold this view said: This is not far-fetched. Do you not see that He commanded the mountains to speak with Dawud, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿O mountains, echo the praises with him, and the birds﴾ [Saba': 10].

Page 94
And Allah the Exalted manifested Himself to the mountain, saying: ﴿So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. And Allah the Exalted made the hands and feet speak, saying: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur: 24]. Since this is so, how is it far-fetched that Allah should create in the very essence of the heaven and the earth life, intellect and understanding, and then direct the command and obligation upon them? This possibility is reinforced by several considerations:

First: the basic principle is to carry the wording upon its apparent meaning unless something prevents it, and here there is no preventer, so it is obligatory to keep it upon its apparent meaning.

Second: He the Exalted informed about them, saying: ﴿They said, "We come obeying"﴾, and this plural is the plural of those who understand and know.

Third: His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72]. This indicates that they recognize Allah and are specifically addressed with the directing of Allah's obligations upon them. The difficulty with this view is that it may be said: what is meant by His saying ﴿Come both of you willingly or unwillingly﴾ is coming into existence, origination and attainment; and on this assumption, at the time this command was directed, the heavens and the earth were non-existent, for if they were existent the result of this command would be to say: "O existent, become existent," and that is not permissible. So it is established that at the time this command was directed to them, they were non-existent, and since they were non-existent they were not comprehending nor aware of the address, so it was not permissible to direct the command to them.

If someone says: Mujahid transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: Allah, glorified is He, said to the heavens: "Bring forth your sun, your moon and your stars," and said to the earth: "Split open your rivers and bring forth your fruits." Allah had deposited these things in them, then commanded them to bring them out and manifest them. We say: on this assumption, the meaning of His saying ﴿We come obeying﴾ is not their origination in their essence; rather the meaning of this command becomes that they should manifest what had been deposited in them. However, this statement is invalid, because He the Exalted said: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾, and the fa' (then) denotes sequence, and this indicates that the origination of the heavens occurred only after His saying: ﴿Come both of you willingly or unwillingly﴾. This is the sum of what can be mentioned in this discussion.

The second view: that His saying the Exalted: ﴿So He said to it and to the earth, "Come both of you willingly or unwillingly"﴾ does not mean directing a command and obligation upon the heavens and the earth; rather it means that He intended their creation, so they did not resist Him, and they came into existence as He willed them. They were in that state like an obedient subordinate when the command of an obeyed commander reaches him. A parallel to this is the saying of one who says: "The wall said to the peg: 'Why do you split me?' The peg said: 'Ask the one who hammers me, for the stone behind me did not leave me alone behind me.'"

Know that this is a departure from the apparent meaning, and departure from the apparent meaning is permitted only when there is evidence that it cannot be carried upon its apparent meaning. We have already shown that His saying ﴿Come both of you willingly or unwillingly﴾ took place before their existence, and when this is the case, it is impossible to take His saying ﴿Come both of you willingly or unwillingly﴾ as a command and obligation; so it is obligatory to interpret it as we have mentioned.

Know that the establishing of command and obligation upon them is conditional on the existence of those commanded in them; and this indicates that He the Exalted settled angels in these heavens, or that He the Exalted commanded them with certain things and forbade them from certain things. There is nothing in the verse indicating that He created the angels together with the heavens, or that He the Exalted created them before the heavens and then settled them therein. Also, there is nothing in the verse explaining the laws (shara'i') with which He commanded the angels; and these secrets are not suited to human intellects, rather they are higher than the ascent of their understandings and the targets of their imaginings.

Then He said: ﴿And We adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾, and they are the luminous bodies which He created in the heavens, and He assigned to each one a specific light, a specific secret, and a specific nature, which none knows except Allah. Then He said: (and as a guard), meaning: and We guarded it with a guarding, meaning from the devils who steal hearing, so He prepared for every devil a star which He throws at him and which never misses him,

of them some burn, some kill, and some render him deranged. It is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that "the Jews asked the Messenger ﷺ about the creation of the heavens and the earth, and he said: 'Allah the Exalted created the earth on Sunday and Monday, created the mountains and trees on two days, created the heaven on Thursday, created on Friday the stars, the sun, the moon and the angels, then created Adam, peace be upon him, and settled him in Paradise.' Then the Jews said: 'Then what, O Muhammad?' He said: 'Then He established Himself upon the Throne.' They said: 'Then He rested,' and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ became angry," so there was revealed His saying the Exalted: ﴿And fatigue did not touch Us﴾ [Qaf: 38].

Know that when He the Exalted mentioned these details, He said: ﴿That is the determination of the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾. "Al-ʿAziz" indicates perfection of power, and "al-ʿAlim" indicates perfection of knowledge; and how excellent this conclusion is, for those works are not possible except with complete power and all-encompassing knowledge.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But if they turn away, then say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd."﴾ ﴿When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them, saying: "Worship none but Allah." They said: "Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels. Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength? And they used to deny Our signs.﴾ ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind in days of misfortune, that We might make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world; but the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgracing, and they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿As for Thamūd, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them for what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah.﴾

Know that the discourse began with His saying ﴿Your God is but one God﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 6], and it was argued for by His saying ﴿Say: "Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days"﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 9]. Its essence is this: how is it permissible to disbelieve in a God described with this overpowering power, and how is it permissible to make these base bodies partners to Him in divinity? When He had completed that argument, He said: ﴿But if they turn away, then say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd."﴾ The explanation of this is that the duty of the argument has been fulfilled in the most complete manner. If they remain persistent in ignorance, then there remains no remedy for them except the sending down of punishment upon them. For this reason He said: ﴿But if they turn away, then say: "I have warned you"﴾, meaning: if they turn away from accepting this overpowering argument which we have mentioned,

[Page 96]

and persist in ignorance and blind imitation, then ﴿say: "I have warned you"﴾. Warning (al-indhār) is intimidation. Al-Mubarrad said: the ṣāʿiqah (thunderbolt) is the destroying bolt, whatever it may be. It was also read as (ṣaʿqatan mithla ṣaʿqati ʿĀdin wa Thamūd). The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, the Qur'anic commentary of al-Zamakhshari) said: it is the single instance of the verb ṣaʿq (a striking down).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them﴾, and in this there are two interpretations:

The first: the meaning is that the messengers sent to them came to them from every side, exerted themselves with them, and employed all manner of stratagems. Yet they saw from them nothing but obstinacy and aversion, just as Allah the Exalted related the words of Satan: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 17], meaning: I will come to them from every direction and will employ every stratagem against them. A man says: "I went around so-and-so from every side, but my stratagem did not affect him."

The second interpretation: the meaning is that the messengers came to them from before them and from after them. If it is said: how is it possible to describe the messengers who came before and after them as having come to them? We say: Hud and Salih came to them calling to belief in them and in all the messengers. By this reckoning, it is as though all the messengers had come to them.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Worship none but Allah﴾, meaning: the messengers who came to them from before them and from behind them commanded them to monotheism and to the negation of association. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the "an" in His saying ﴿an lā taʿbudū illā Allāh﴾ is in the sense of "ay" (that), or it is the light form of the heavy (an, with the verb in the subjunctive), its original form being "annahu lā taʿbudū", that is: the matter and the discourse is our saying to you: do not worship except Allah.

Then Allah the Exalted related of those disbelievers that they said: ﴿Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels﴾, meaning that they denied those messengers and said: the proof that they are liars is that if God the Exalted had willed to send the message to mankind, He would have made His messengers from the company of the angels, because the sending of angels to creation would have led more directly to the purpose of prophethood and messengership.

When they mentioned this doubt, they said ﴿So we disbelieve in what you have been sent with﴾. Its meaning: since you are humans and not angels, then you are not messengers. And if you are not messengers, we are not obliged to accept your word. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿So we disbelieve in what you have been sent with﴾.

Know that we have elaborated in answering these doubts in surah al-Anʿām. His saying ﴿what you have been sent with﴾ is not an acknowledgment by them that those prophets were messengers; rather, they mentioned it either by way of relating the words of the messengers or as a form of mockery, just as Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 27].

It is narrated that Abu Jahl said in an assembly of Quraysh: "The matter of Muhammad has become confused for us. So if you find for us a man learned in poetry, magic and soothsaying, let him speak with him and then bring us an explanation of his affair." ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah said: "By Allah, I have heard poetry, magic and soothsaying, and I have knowledge of these things, and nothing of them is hidden from me." So he went to him and said: "O Muhammad, are you better, or Hashim? Are you better, or ʿAbd al-Muttalib? Are you better, or ʿAbdullah? Why do you revile our gods and mislead us? If you want leadership, we will raise the banner for you and you will be our chief; and if it is marriage you desire, we will marry you to ten women, choosing whichever daughters of Quraysh you wish; and if wealth is your aim, we will gather for you what will make you rich." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained silent. When he had finished, he said: "In the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful. Ḥā Mīm. A revelation from the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful..." up to His saying "a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd." ʿUtbah then put his hand over his mouth and implored him by the ties of kinship, and returned to his family and did not go out to Quraysh. When he was delayed from them, they said: "We see that ʿUtbah has only apostatized." So they went to him and said: "O ʿUtbah, what has kept you from us except that you have apostatized?" He became angry and swore that he would never speak to Muhammad again. Then he said: "By Allah, I did speak to him, and he answered me with something that is neither poetry, nor magic, nor soothsaying. When he reached 'a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd', I put my hand over his mouth and implored him by the ties of kinship, for I knew that Muhammad, when he says something, does not lie, and I feared that the punishment would descend upon you."

Know that when He had clarified in general the disbelief of the peoples of ʿĀd and Thamūd, He then clarified the particular characteristic of each of these two groups. He said: ﴿As for ʿĀd, they were arrogant in the land without right﴾. This arrogance has two interpretations:

The first: displaying pride and haughtiness, and not paying attention to others.

The second: exalting oneself over others and making them subservient.

Then Allah the Exalted mentioned the cause of that arrogance, which is that they said: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ They were distinguished by the largeness of their bodies and the intensity of their strength. Then He the Exalted mentioned what indicates that it is not permissible for them to be deceived by the intensity of their strength. He said: ﴿Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ Meaning: though they were stronger than others, Allah who created them is mightier than them in strength. If increase in strength makes the weaker one obedient to the stronger, then this relationship obliges them to be submissive to Allah the Exalted, humbled before His commands and prohibitions.

Our companions have used this verse to establish power for Allah. They said: strength belongs to Allah the Exalted. This is reinforced by His saying ﴿Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength﴾, which indicates the affirmation of strength for Allah the Exalted. This is further reinforced by His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 58]. If it is said: the form of the comparative (ifʿal al-tafḍīl) applies only between two things where one has a relation to the other, but the power of the servant is finite and the power of Allah has no end, and the finite has no relation to the infinite, so what is the meaning of His saying that Allah is mightier than them in strength? We say: this came in the manner of our saying "Allahu akbar" (Allah is greater).

Then He said: ﴿And they used to deny Our signs﴾. The meaning is that they knew that they were true, but they denied them just as a trustee denies a deposit.

Know that the structure of the speech would be: "As for ʿĀd, they were arrogant in the land without right, and they used to deny Our signs." His saying ﴿and said: "Who is mightier than us in strength? Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?"﴾ is a parenthetical insertion placed in between to establish the cause that moved them to arrogance.

Know that we have mentioned that the comprehensive qualities of praiseworthy character are (doing good to creation and glorifying the Creator). His saying ﴿they were arrogant in the land without right﴾ is contrary to doing good to creation, and His saying ﴿and they used to deny Our signs﴾ is contrary to glorifying the Creator. Since this is so, they had reached the furthest extent in the blameworthy attributes that bring about destruction and ruin. For this reason Allah imposed the punishment upon them. He said: ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind﴾. As for ṣarṣar (furious), there are two views:

One: that it is the violent storm that makes a ṣarṣara sound, meaning it produces a sound in its blowing. Regarding the reason for this name there are several views: it is said that when winds blow intensely, a sound is heard from them resembling the sound of ṣarṣar, so these winds were named by this name. It is also said that it derives from the creaking of a door (ṣarīr al-bāb), and it is said that it derives from ṣarra (a cry) and ṣayḥa (a shout). From this is His saying: ﴿Then his wife came forward in a cry﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 29].

The second view: that it is the cold wind which burns with its cold just as fire burns with its heat. Its origin is from ṣirr, which is cold. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Like a wind in which is a bitter cold﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 117]. And it is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The winds are eight: four of them are punishment: the violent (al-ʿāṣif), the ṣarṣar, the barren (al-ʿaqīm), and the simoom (al-samūm); and four of them are mercy: those that spread the clouds (al-nāshirāt), those that bring good tidings (al-mubashshirāt), those that are sent (al-mursalāt), and those that scatter (al-dhāriyāt)." And it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that Allah the Exalted did not send upon His servants of wind except the measure of my ring. The point is that, despite its smallness, it destroyed everything, and this indicates the perfection of His power.

The second: exalting oneself over others and making them subservient.

Then Allah the Exalted mentioned the cause of that arrogance, which is that they said: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ They were distinguished by the largeness of their bodies and the intensity of their strength. * * *

Then He said: ﴿And they used to deny Our signs﴾. The meaning is that they knew that they were true, but they denied them just as a trustee denies a deposit.

And it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that Allah the Exalted did not send upon His servants of wind except the measure of my ring. The point is that, despite its smallness, it destroyed everything, and this indicates the perfection of His power.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 41, verses 13–15:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But if they turn away, then say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd."﴾ ﴿When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them, saying: "Worship none but Allah." They said: "Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels. So we disbelieve in what you have been sent with."﴾ ﴿As for ʿĀd, they were arrogant in the land without right and said: "Who is mightier than us in strength?" Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength? And they used to deny Our signs.﴾ ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind in days of misfortune, that We might make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world; but the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgracing, and they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿As for Thamūd, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them for what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah.﴾

Know that the discourse began with His saying ﴿Your God is but one God﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 6], and it was argued for by His saying ﴿Say: "Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days"﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 9]. Its essence is this: how is it permissible to disbelieve in a God described with this overpowering power, and how is it permissible to make these base bodies partners to Him in divinity? When He had completed that argument, He said: ﴿But if they turn away, then say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd."﴾ The explanation of this is that the duty of the argument has been fulfilled in the most complete manner. If they remain persistent in ignorance, then there remains no remedy for them except the sending down of punishment upon them. For this reason He said: ﴿But if they turn away, then say: "I have warned you"﴾, meaning: if they turn away from accepting this overpowering argument which we have mentioned,

[Page 96]

and persist in ignorance and blind imitation, then ﴿say: "I have warned you"﴾. Warning (al-indhār) is intimidation. Al-Mubarrad said: the ṣāʿiqah (thunderbolt) is the destroying bolt, whatever it may be. It was also read as (ṣaʿqatan mithla ṣaʿqati ʿĀdin wa Thamūd). The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, the Qur'anic commentary of al-Zamakhshari) said: it is the single instance of the verb ṣaʿq (a striking down).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them﴾, and in this there are two interpretations:

The first: the meaning is that the messengers sent to them came to them from every side, exerted themselves with them, and employed all manner of stratagems. Yet they saw from them nothing but obstinacy and aversion, just as Allah the Exalted related the words of Satan: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 17], meaning: I will come to them from every direction and will employ every stratagem against them. A man says: "I went around so-and-so from every side, but my stratagem did not affect him."

The second interpretation: the meaning is that the messengers came to them from before them and from after them. If it is said: how is it possible to describe the messengers who came before and after them as having come to them? We say: Hud and Salih came to them calling to belief in them and in all the messengers. By this reckoning, it is as though all the messengers had come to them.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Worship none but Allah﴾, meaning: the messengers who came to them from before them and from behind them commanded them to monotheism and to the negation of association. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the "an" in His saying ﴿an lā taʿbudū illā Allāh﴾ is in the sense of "ay" (that), or it is the light form of the heavy (an, with the verb in the subjunctive), its original form being "annahu lā taʿbudū", that is: the matter and the discourse is our saying to you: do not worship except Allah.

Then Allah the Exalted related of those disbelievers that they said: ﴿Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels﴾, meaning that they denied those messengers and said: the proof that they are liars is that if God the Exalted had willed to send the message to mankind, He would have made His messengers from the company of the angels, because the sending of angels to creation would have led more directly to the purpose of prophethood and messengership.

When they mentioned this doubt, they said ﴿So we disbelieve in what you have been sent with﴾. Its meaning: since you are humans and not angels, then you are not messengers. And if you are not messengers, we are not obliged to accept your word. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿So we disbelieve in what you have been sent with﴾.

Know that we have elaborated in answering these doubts in surah al-Anʿām. His saying ﴿what you have been sent with﴾ is not an acknowledgment by them that those prophets were messengers; rather, they mentioned it either by way of relating the words of the messengers or as a form of mockery, just as Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 27].

It is narrated that Abu Jahl said in an assembly of Quraysh: "The matter of Muhammad has become confused for us. So if you find for us a man learned in poetry, magic and soothsaying, let him speak with him and then bring us an explanation of his affair." ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah said: "By Allah, I have heard poetry, magic and soothsaying, and I have knowledge of these things, and nothing of them is hidden from me." So he went to him and said: "O Muhammad, are you better, or Hashim? Are you better, or ʿAbd al-Muttalib? Are you better, or ʿAbdullah? Why do you revile our gods and mislead us? If you want leadership, we will raise the banner for you and you will be our chief; and if it is marriage you desire, we will marry you to ten women, choosing whichever daughters of Quraysh you wish; and if wealth is your aim, we will gather for you what will make you rich." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained silent. When he had finished, he said: "In the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful. Ḥā Mīm. A revelation from the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful..." up to His saying "a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd." ʿUtbah then put his hand over his mouth and implored him by the ties of kinship, and returned to his family and did not go out to Quraysh. When he was delayed from them, they said: "We see that ʿUtbah has only apostatized." So they went to him and said: "O ʿUtbah, what has kept you from us except that you have apostatized?" He became angry and swore that he would never speak to Muhammad again. Then he said: "By Allah, I did speak to him, and he answered me with something that is neither poetry, nor magic, nor soothsaying. When he reached 'a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd', I put my hand over his mouth and implored him by the ties of kinship, for I knew that Muhammad, when he says something, does not lie, and I feared that the punishment would descend upon you."
