[p. 98]

As for His saying ﴿in days of ill omen﴾, there are several issues.

**First issue:** Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "nahsat" (نَحْسَاتٍ) with a sukun on the ha' (ح), while the rest read it with a kasrah (نَحِسَاتٍ). The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: It is said "nahisa nahsan," the opposite of "sa'ida sa'dan," so the one is "nahis" (نَحِسٌ). As for "nahs" (نَحْسٌ), it is either a lightened form of "nahis," or an adjective of the pattern "fa'l," or a description using a verbal noun (maṣdar).

**Second issue:** The judicial astrologers (al-Ahkamiyyun, those who hold that the stars determine events) among the astrologers (al-Munajjimin) cited this verse as evidence that some days are ill-omened and some days are auspicious. They said: this verse is explicit in this meaning. The theologians (al-Mutakallimun) replied by saying: ﴿in days of ill omen﴾ means days full of dust and of raging sand, in which one can hardly see or move about. Also, they said: the meaning of these days being ill-omened is that God destroyed them in them. The first party who cited the evidence replied that "nahisat" in the linguistic usage means "unlucky," because "sa'd" (good fortune) is opposed by "sa'd" (its own opposite term in this usage), and "kadir" (turbid) is opposed by "safi" (clear). He answered the second question by saying: God, Exalted is He, informed us that the punishment was inflicted in those ill-omened days, so the fact that those days were ill-omened must be different from the punishment that occurred in them.

* * *

Then God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿that We might make them taste the punishment of humiliation in the life of this world﴾, i.e., the punishment of disgrace and abasement. The cause of it was that they were arrogant, so God met that arrogance by bringing upon them disgrace, humiliation and abasement.

* * *

Then God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more humiliating﴾, i.e., more severe in disgrace and degradation, ﴿and they will not be helped﴾, i.e., they will suffer the severe disgrace, and along with that there will be no helper to repel that disgrace from them.

When God mentioned the story of 'Ad, He followed it with the story of Thamud. He said: ﴿And as for Thamud﴾. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "Thamud" has been read in the nominative (raf') and accusative (nasb), both with and without tanwin (nunation). The nominative is more eloquent, because it comes after the particle of inception (ḥarf al-ibtida'). It has also been read with a ḍammah on the thā' (ثَمُودُ, read as Thumud). As for His saying ﴿so We guided them﴾, i.e., We showed them the path of good and evil. ﴿But they preferred blindness over guidance﴾, i.e., they chose to enter misguidance over entering right guidance.

Know that the author of *al-Kashshaf* explained the word "guidance" (al-huda) in His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah 2] as an indication that leads to the desired goal. This verse refutes his statement, because it shows that guidance has been attained even though arrival at the desired goal was not attained. Thus it is established that the condition of its leading to the goal is not required in the meaning of the name "guidance."

There is a question that arises from this verse, which points to this, but he did not give a satisfying answer, so we have left it aside. The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites, a theological school) said: this verse indicates that God, Exalted is He, may set up proofs and remove excuses and causes, but faith arises only from the servant, because His saying ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them﴾ indicates that He set up proofs for them, and His saying ﴿but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ indicates that they, of their own selves, brought about that blindness. Hence this indicates that both disbelief and faith arise from the servant. I say: rather, this verse is among the strongest proofs that both of them arise from God and not from the servant. Its explanation is in two respects:

The first: The blindness proceeded from them only because they loved to acquire it. When this love arose in their hearts rather than the love of its opposite, if that preponderance occurred without a determining cause, it is invalid. If the determining factor was the servant, the question returns. If the determining factor was God, then what is sought has been achieved.

The second: He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾, and it is known by necessity that no one loves blindness and ignorance while knowing that they are blindness and ignorance. Rather, whoever does not believe that such blindness and ignorance is insight and knowledge does not desire it. So his undertaking to choose that ignorance must be preceded by another ignorance. If that second ignorance was also chosen by him, this leads to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. Therefore those ignorances must end in an ignorance that arises in him not by his choice, and that is what was sought.

When God described their disbelief, He said: ﴿So the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them﴾. ﴿Thunderbolt of punishment﴾ means the calamity of punishment, and "al-Hun" (الهُونِ) means humiliation. The punishment was described by it for emphasis, or it was put in apposition to it. ﴿For what they used to earn﴾ means: on account of their polytheism, their denial of Salih, and their hamstringing of the she-camel. The author of *al-Kashshaf* here embarked on a great folly, and it is best not to pay attention to him, because although he made a fine effort concerning the wording, that poor man was far from the meanings.

When God mentioned the threat, He followed it with the promise, and said: ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear God﴾, meaning: and they used to avoid the deeds which the people of 'Ad and Thamud used to commit. If it is asked: how is it permissible for the Messenger ﷺ to warn his people with a punishment like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud, while knowing that such a thing does not occur among the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ? God, Exalted is He, has affirmed this in His saying ﴿But God would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal 33], and authentic hadiths report that God lifted these kinds of calamities from this Ummah. We say: when they recognized that they were sharers with 'Ad and Thamud in deserving a thunderbolt like theirs, they considered the occurrence of something of the same kind possible, even if it was of a lesser degree than theirs. This amount is sufficient for warning.

[p. 98]

As for His saying ﴿in days of ill omen﴾, there are several issues.

**First issue:** Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "nahsat" (نَحْسَاتٍ) with a sukun on the ha' (ح), while the rest read it with a kasrah (نَحِسَاتٍ). The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: It is said "nahisa nahsan," the opposite of "sa'ida sa'dan," so the one is "nahis" (نَحِسٌ). As for "nahs" (نَحْسٌ), it is either a lightened form of "nahis," or an adjective of the pattern "fa'l," or a description using a verbal noun (maṣdar).

**Second issue:** The judicial astrologers (al-Ahkamiyyun, those who hold that the stars determine events) among the astrologers (al-Munajjimin) cited this verse as evidence that some days are ill-omened and some days are auspicious. They said: this verse is explicit in this meaning. The theologians (al-Mutakallimun) replied by saying: ﴿in days of ill omen﴾ means days full of dust and of raging sand, in which one can hardly see or move about. Also, they said: the meaning of these days being ill-omened is that God destroyed them in them. The first party who cited the evidence replied that "nahisat" in the linguistic usage means "unlucky," because "sa'd" (good fortune) is opposed by "sa'd" (its own opposite term in this usage), and "kadir" (turbid) is opposed by "safi" (clear). He answered the second question by saying: God, Exalted is He, informed us that the punishment was inflicted in those ill-omened days, so the fact that those days were ill-omened must be different from the punishment that occurred in them.

* * *

Then God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿that We might make them taste the punishment of humiliation in the life of this world﴾, i.e., the punishment of disgrace and abasement. The cause of it was that they were arrogant, so God met that arrogance by bringing upon them disgrace, humiliation and abasement.

* * *

Then God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more humiliating﴾, i.e., more severe in disgrace and degradation, ﴿and they will not be helped﴾, i.e., they will suffer the severe disgrace, and along with that there will be no helper to repel that disgrace from them.

When God mentioned the story of 'Ad, He followed it with the story of Thamud. He said: ﴿And as for Thamud﴾. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "Thamud" has been read in the nominative (raf') and accusative (nasb), both with and without tanwin (nunation). The nominative is more eloquent, because it comes after the particle of inception (ḥarf al-ibtida'). It has also been read with a ḍammah on the thā' (ثَمُودُ, read as Thumud). As for His saying ﴿so We guided them﴾, i.e., We showed them the path of good and evil. ﴿But they preferred blindness over guidance﴾, i.e., they chose to enter misguidance over entering right guidance.

Know that the author of *al-Kashshaf* explained the word "guidance" (al-huda) in His saying ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah 2] as an indication that leads to the desired goal. This verse refutes his statement, because it shows that guidance has been attained even though arrival at the desired goal was not attained. Thus it is established that the condition of its leading to the goal is not required in the meaning of the name "guidance."

There is a question that arises from this verse, which points to this, but he did not give a satisfying answer, so we have left it aside. The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites, a theological school) said: this verse indicates that God, Exalted is He, may set up proofs and remove excuses and causes, but faith arises only from the servant, because His saying ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them﴾ indicates that He set up proofs for them, and His saying ﴿but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ indicates that they, of their own selves, brought about that blindness. Hence this indicates that both disbelief and faith arise from the servant. I say: rather, this verse is among the strongest proofs that both of them arise from God and not from the servant. Its explanation is in two respects:

The first: The blindness proceeded from them only because they loved to acquire it. When this love arose in their hearts rather than the love of its opposite, if that preponderance occurred without a determining cause, it is invalid. If the determining factor was the servant, the question returns. If the determining factor was God, then what is sought has been achieved.

The second: He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾, and it is known by necessity that no one loves blindness and ignorance while knowing that they are blindness and ignorance. Rather, whoever does not believe that such blindness and ignorance is insight and knowledge does not desire it. So his undertaking to choose that ignorance must be preceded by another ignorance. If that second ignorance was also chosen by him, this leads to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. Therefore those ignorances must end in an ignorance that arises in him not by his choice, and that is what was sought.

When God described their disbelief, He said: ﴿So the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them﴾. ﴿Thunderbolt of punishment﴾ means the calamity of punishment, and "al-Hun" (الهُونِ) means humiliation. The punishment was described by it for emphasis, or it was put in apposition to it. ﴿For what they used to earn﴾ means: on account of their polytheism, their denial of Salih, and their hamstringing of the she-camel. The author of *al-Kashshaf* here embarked on a great folly, and it is best not to pay attention to him, because although he made a fine effort concerning the wording, that poor man was far from the meanings.

When God mentioned the threat, He followed it with the promise, and said: ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear God﴾, meaning: and they used to avoid the deeds which the people of 'Ad and Thamud used to commit. We say: when they recognized that they were sharers with 'Ad and Thamud in deserving a thunderbolt like theirs, they considered the occurrence of something of the same kind possible, even if it was of a lesser degree than theirs. This amount is sufficient for warning.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 41, verse 19–24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire, they will be driven in groups.﴾ ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them concerning what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?" They will say, "Allah has caused us to speak, who causes everything to speak, and He created you the first time, and to Him you are returned."﴾ ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins should testify against you, but you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do.﴾ ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has brought you to ruin, and you have become among the losers.﴾ ﴿So if they are patient, the Fire is their residence; and if they ask to be reconciled, they will not be among those reconciled.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained the manner of the punishment of those disbelievers in this world, He followed it with the manner of their punishment in the Hereafter, so that the lesson in warning and admonition would be complete.

Nafi' read "nahshuru" (We gather) with a nun, and "a'da'" (enemies) in the accusative, attributing the gathering to Himself. The implied meaning is: Allah, mighty and majestic, gathers His enemies, the disbelievers, from the first and the last. His argument is that it is coordinated with His saying: "and We saved" (Fussilat 18), so it is fitting that it be in agreement with it in wording. It is strengthened by His saying: "the Day We gather the God-fearing" and "and We gathered them." As for the others, they recited it in the passive form (fi'l ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu), because the story of Thamud had ended, and His saying "and on the Day when He is gathered" is the beginning of another statement. Also, those who gather them are those commanded by His saying "Gather together" (al-Saffat 22), and they are the angels. Also, this recitation agrees with His saying "so they are driven in groups." Also, the implied meaning of the first recitation would be that Allah, exalted, said: "And on the Day We gather the enemies of Allah to the Fire," and on this reading it would have been better to say: "And on the Day We gather our enemies to the Fire."

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire, He said: ﴿so they are driven in groups﴾, meaning their first is held back until their last, that is, their predecessors are halted until their followers reach them. The purpose is to show that when they assemble they are questioned about their deeds.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them﴾. In this there are several issues:

The first issue: the implied meaning is "until, when they come to Us, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them." On this reading the word "ma" is superfluous (silah). It has been said that it has an additional function, namely to emphasise that at the time of their arrival this testimony must occur, as in His saying: "Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it?" (Yunus 51), meaning that the time of its occurrence must be the time of their belief in it.

The second issue: it is reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The servant will say on the Day of Resurrection: 'O Lord of might, did You not promise me that You would not wrong me?' Allah, exalted, will say: 'Indeed, that is so.' The servant will say: 'I do not accept any witness against myself except from myself.' So Allah will seal his mouth and cause his limbs to speak of the deeds that proceeded from him. That is His saying: 'Their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them.'"

People differed concerning the manner of the testimony, and on this there are three opinions:

The first: He creates in them understanding, power and speech, so they testify as a man testifies to what he knows.

The second: He creates in those limbs sounds and letters that indicate those meanings, just as He created speech in the tree.

The third: those limbs display states which indicate that those deeds proceeded from that person, and those signs are called testimonies, just as it is said that this world testifies by the changes of its states to its having been created. Know that this question is difficult for the Mu'tazilah.

As for the first opinion, it is difficult according to their doctrine, because structure (bunyah) is for them a condition for the occurrence of intellect and power. The tongue, insofar as it is a tongue, cannot be a locus of knowledge and intellect. If Allah changed that structure and form, it would cease to be a tongue or a skin. The apparent meaning of the verse attributes that testimony to the hearing, the sight and the skins. If we say that Allah did not change the structure of these limbs, then it is impossible for them to be speaking and understanding.

As for the second opinion, which is to say that Allah created these sounds and letters in these limbs, this is also false according to the principles of the Mu'tazilah, because their doctrine is that the one who speaks is the one who produced the speech, not that which is described as speaking. For they say that Allah created speech in the tree, and the one speaking by that speech was Allah, not the tree. Here, if we say that Allah created the sounds and letters in those limbs, it would follow that the witness is Allah, not those, and that the speaker of those words is Allah, not those limbs. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that this testimony is a testimony that proceeded from those limbs, not from Allah, exalted; for He said: "Their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them." Also, they said to those limbs: "Why did you testify against us?" and the limbs said: "Allah has caused us to speak, who causes everything to speak." All these verses indicate that the one speaking those words is those limbs, and that those words are not the speech of Allah, exalted. This is the explanation of the difficulty in these two opinions.

As for the third opinion, which is to interpret this testimony as the appearance of specific signs on these limbs indicating that those deeds proceeded from them, this is a departure from the literal meaning to the figurative, and the default is its absence. This is the end of the discussion on this topic.

According to the doctrine of our companions, this difficulty does not arise, because for us structure is not a condition for life, nor for knowledge, nor for power. Allah, exalted, is able to create intellect, power and speech in every part of these limbs. On this assumption the difficulty disappears, and this verse may fittingly be cited to show that structure is not a condition for life, nor for any of the attributes conditioned upon life. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: I have not seen among the exegetes any reason or benefit for singling out these three limbs for mention. I say: there is no doubt that the senses are five: hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch. And there is no doubt that the instrument of touch is the skin. Allah, exalted, mentioned here three of the senses: hearing, sight and touch, and omitted two kinds: taste and smell. Taste is included in touch in some respects, because the perception of taste is only achieved when the skin of the tongue and the palate touches the substance of the food, so this is included within it. There remains the sense of smell, which is a weak sense in man, and for which Allah has no obligation, command or prohibition. Knowing this, we say: it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "What is meant by the testimony of the skins is the testimony of the private parts." He said: "This is by way of metaphor (kinayat), as He said: 'But do not promise them in secret' (al-Baqarah 235), meaning marriage, and He said: 'Or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself' (al-Nisa' 43), meaning relieving oneself."

And from the Prophet ﷺ it is reported that he said: "The first part of the son of Adam to speak is his thigh and his palm." On this assumption this verse is a severe warning against committing fornication, because the preliminary of fornication is achieved by the hand, and its ultimate stage is achieved by the thigh.

Then Allah, exalted, related that they will say to those limbs: ﴿Why did you testify against us?﴾ They will say: ﴿Allah has caused us to speak, who causes everything to speak, and He created you the first time, and to Him you are returned.﴾ The meaning is that He who is able to create you and cause you to speak the first time, while you were in this world, and then to create you and cause you to speak the second time, which is the state of the Resurrection and the Resurrection, is it far-fetched that He should cause the limbs and organs to speak?

* * *

Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins should testify against you﴾. The meaning is the affirmation that they used to conceal themselves when undertaking evil deeds, but their concealment was not out of fear that their hearing, their sight and their skins would testify against them, because they denied the Resurrection and the Last Day. Rather, that concealment was because they thought that Allah does not know the deeds they undertook in secrecy and concealment.

From Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I was hidden behind the curtains of the Ka'bah, when three men entered: two Thaqafis and a Qurashi. One of them said: 'Do you think Allah hears what we say?' The two men said: 'If we raise our voices He hears, and if not, He does not hear.' I mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and there was revealed: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves...﴾"

* * *

Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has brought you to ruin, and you have become among the losers.﴾ This is an explicit text that whoever assumes about Allah, exalted, that some of the known things escape His knowledge, will be among the ruined losers. The people of verification (ahl al-tahqiq) said: assumption (zann) is of two kinds: a good assumption about Allah, exalted, and a corrupt assumption. As for the good assumption, it is that one assumes of Him mercy and bounty. The Prophet ﷺ said, relating from Allah, mighty and majestic: "I am according to My servant's assumption of Me." And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Let none of you die except while he has a good assumption of Allah." As for the evil assumption, it is corrupt, and it is that one assumes of Allah that some of these states escape His knowledge. Qatadah said: assumption is of two kinds: a saving assumption and a destructive assumption. The saving one is His saying: "Indeed I assumed that I would meet my reckoning" (al-Haqqah 20), and His saying: "Those who assume that they will meet their Lord" (al-Baqarah 46). As for the destructive assumption, it is His saying: "And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord." The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Dhalikum" is in the nominative as the subject, and "zannukum" and "ardakum" are two predicates; it is also permissible that "zannukum" be a substitute for "dhalikum," and "ardakum" the predicate.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So if they are patient, the Fire is their residence﴾, meaning: if they refrain from seeking relief for a deliverance they are awaiting, they will not find it, and the Fire will be their residence, that is, their place of abode. ﴿And if they ask to be reconciled, they will not be among those reconciled﴾, meaning they will not be granted reconciliation (al-'utbā) and will not be answered in it. A parallel to this is His saying: "Whether we rage or endure patiently, there is no escape for us" (Ibrahim 21). It has also been recited: "wa in yasta'tibu fa-ma hum mina al-mu'tabin," meaning: if they ask to satisfy their Lord, they will not be doing so, that is, there is no way for them to that.

Then Allah, exalted, related that they will say to those limbs: ﴿Why did you testify against us?﴾ They will say: ﴿Allah has caused us to speak, who causes everything to speak, and He created you the first time, and to Him you are returned.﴾ The meaning is that He who is able to create you and cause you to speak the first time, while you were in this world, and then to create you and cause you to speak the second time, which is the state of the Resurrection and the Resurrection, is it far-fetched that He should cause the limbs and organs to speak?

* * *

Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins should testify against you﴾. The meaning is the affirmation that they used to conceal themselves when undertaking evil deeds, but their concealment was not out of fear that their hearing, their sight and their skins would testify against them, because they denied the Resurrection and the Last Day. Rather, that concealment was because they thought that Allah does not know the deeds they undertook in secrecy and concealment.

From Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I was hidden behind the curtains of the Ka'bah, when three men entered: two Thaqafis and a Qurashi. One of them said: 'Do you think Allah hears what we say?' The two men said: 'If we raise our voices He hears, and if not, He does not hear.' I mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and there was revealed: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves...﴾"

* * *

Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has brought you to ruin, and you have become among the losers.﴾ This is an explicit text that whoever assumes about Allah, exalted, that some of the known things escape His knowledge, will be among the ruined losers. The people of verification (ahl al-tahqiq) said: assumption (zann) is of two kinds: a good assumption about Allah, exalted, and a corrupt assumption. As for the good assumption, it is that one assumes of Him mercy and bounty. The Prophet ﷺ said, relating from Allah, mighty and majestic: "I am according to My servant's assumption of Me." And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Let none of you die except while he has a good assumption of Allah." As for the evil assumption, it is corrupt, and it is that one assumes of Allah that some of these states escape His knowledge. Qatadah said: assumption is of two kinds: a saving assumption and a destructive assumption. The saving one is His saying: "Indeed I assumed that I would meet my reckoning" (al-Haqqah 20), and His saying: "Those who assume that they will meet their Lord" (al-Baqarah 46). As for the destructive assumption, it is His saying: "And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord." The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Dhalikum" is in the nominative as the subject, and "zannukum" and "ardakum" are two predicates; it is also permissible that "zannukum" be a substitute for "dhalikum," and "ardakum" the predicate.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So if they are patient, the Fire is their residence﴾, meaning: if they refrain from seeking relief for a deliverance they are awaiting, they will not find it, and the Fire will be their residence, that is, their place of abode. ﴿And if they ask to be reconciled, they will not be among those reconciled﴾, meaning they will not be granted reconciliation (al-'utbā) and will not be answered in it. A parallel to this is His saying: "Whether we rage or endure patiently, there is no escape for us" (Ibrahim 21). It has also been recited: "wa in yasta'tibu fa-ma hum mina al-mu'tabin," meaning: if they ask to satisfy their Lord, they will not be doing so, that is, there is no way for them to that.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 41, verse 19–24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire, they will be driven in groups.﴾ ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them concerning what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?" They will say, "Allah has caused us to speak, who causes everything to speak, and He created you the first time, and to Him you are returned."﴾ ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins should testify against you, but you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do.﴾ ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has brought you to ruin, and you have become among the losers.﴾ ﴿So if they are patient, the Fire is their residence; and if they ask to be reconciled, they will not be among those reconciled.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained the manner of the punishment of those disbelievers in this world, He followed it with the manner of their punishment in the Hereafter, so that the lesson in warning and admonition would be complete.

Nafi' read "nahshuru" (We gather) with a nun, and "a'da'" (enemies) in the accusative, attributing the gathering to Himself. The implied meaning is: Allah, mighty and majestic, gathers His enemies, the disbelievers, from the first and the last. His argument is that it is coordinated with His saying: "and We saved" (Fussilat 18), so it is fitting that it be in agreement with it in wording. It is strengthened by His saying: "the Day We gather the God-fearing" and "and We gathered them." As for the others, they recited it in the passive form (fi'l ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu), because the story of Thamud had ended, and His saying "and on the Day when He is gathered" is the beginning of another statement. Also, those who gather them are those commanded by His saying "Gather together" (al-Saffat 22), and they are the angels. Also, this recitation agrees with His saying "so they are driven in groups." Also, the implied meaning of the first recitation would be that Allah, exalted, said: "And on the Day We gather the enemies of Allah to the Fire," and on this reading it would have been better to say: "And on the Day We gather our enemies to the Fire."

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire, He said: ﴿so they are driven in groups﴾, meaning their first is held back until their last, that is, their predecessors are halted until their followers reach them. The purpose is to show that when they assemble they are questioned about their deeds.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them﴾. In this there are several issues:

The first issue: the implied meaning is "until, when they come to Us, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them." On this reading the word "ma" is superfluous (silah). It has been said that it has an additional function, namely to emphasise that at the time of their arrival this testimony must occur, as in His saying: "Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it?" (Yunus 51), meaning that the time of its occurrence must be the time of their belief in it.

The second issue: it is reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The servant will say on the Day of Resurrection: 'O Lord of might, did You not promise me that You would not wrong me?' Allah, exalted, will say: 'Indeed, that is so.' The servant will say: 'I do not accept any witness against myself except from myself.' So Allah will seal his mouth and cause his limbs to speak of the deeds that proceeded from him. That is His saying: 'Their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them.'"

People differed concerning the manner of the testimony, and on this there are three opinions:

The first: He creates in them understanding, power and speech, so they testify as a man testifies to what he knows.

The second: He creates in those limbs sounds and letters that indicate those meanings, just as He created speech in the tree.

The third: those limbs display states which indicate that those deeds proceeded from that person, and those signs are called testimonies, just as it is said that this world testifies by the changes of its states to its having been created. Know that this question is difficult for the Mu'tazilah.

As for the first opinion, it is difficult according to their doctrine, because structure (bunyah) is for them a condition for the occurrence of intellect and power. The tongue, insofar as it is a tongue, cannot be a locus of knowledge and intellect. If Allah changed that structure and form, it would cease to be a tongue or a skin. The apparent meaning of the verse attributes that testimony to the hearing, the sight and the skins. If we say that Allah did not change the structure of these limbs, then it is impossible for them to be speaking and understanding.

As for the second opinion, which is to say that Allah created these sounds and letters in these limbs, this is also false according to the principles of the Mu'tazilah, because their doctrine is that the one who speaks is the one who produced the speech, not that which is described as speaking. For they say that Allah created speech in the tree, and the one speaking by that speech was Allah, not the tree. Here, if we say that Allah created the sounds and letters in those limbs, it would follow that the witness is Allah, not those, and that the speaker of those words is Allah, not those limbs. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that this testimony is a testimony that proceeded from those limbs, not from Allah, exalted; for He said: "Their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them." Also, they said to those limbs: "Why did you testify against us?" and the limbs said: "Allah has caused us to speak, who causes everything to speak." All these verses indicate that the one speaking those words is those limbs, and that those words are not the speech of Allah, exalted. This is the explanation of the difficulty in these two opinions.

As for the third opinion, which is to interpret this testimony as the appearance of specific signs on these limbs indicating that those deeds proceeded from them, this is a departure from the literal meaning to the figurative, and the default is its absence. This is the end of the discussion on this topic.

According to the doctrine of our companions, this difficulty does not arise, because for us structure is not a condition for life, nor for knowledge, nor for power. Allah, exalted, is able to create intellect, power and speech in every part of these limbs. On this assumption the difficulty disappears, and this verse may fittingly be cited to show that structure is not a condition for life, nor for any of the attributes conditioned upon life. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: I have not seen among the exegetes any reason or benefit for singling out these three limbs for mention. I say: there is no doubt that the senses are five: hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch. And there is no doubt that the instrument of touch is the skin. Allah, exalted, mentioned here three of the senses: hearing, sight and touch, and omitted two kinds: taste and smell. Taste is included in touch in some respects, because the perception of taste is only achieved when the skin of the tongue and the palate touches the substance of the food, so this is included within it. There remains the sense of smell, which is a weak sense in man, and for which Allah has no obligation, command or prohibition. Knowing this, we say: it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "What is meant by the testimony of the skins is the testimony of the private parts." He said: "This is by way of metaphor (kinayat), as He said: 'But do not promise them in secret' (al-Baqarah 235), meaning marriage, and He said: 'Or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself' (al-Nisa' 43), meaning relieving oneself."

And from the Prophet ﷺ it is reported that he said: "The first part of the son of Adam to speak is his thigh and his palm." On this assumption this verse is a severe warning against committing fornication, because the preliminary of fornication is achieved by the hand, and its ultimate stage is achieved by the thigh.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So if they are patient, the Fire is their residence﴾, meaning: if they refrain from seeking relief for a deliverance they are awaiting, they will not find it, and the Fire will be their residence, that is, their place of abode. ﴿And if they ask to be reconciled, they will not be among those reconciled﴾, meaning they will not be granted reconciliation (al-'utbā) and will not be answered in it. A parallel to this is His saying: "Whether we rage or endure patiently, there is no escape for us" (Ibrahim 21). It has also been recited: "wa in yasta'tibu fa-ma hum mina al-mu'tabin," meaning: if they ask to satisfy their Lord, they will not be doing so, that is, there is no way for them to that.

He, exalted is He, said: "And We appointed for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them, and the Word became due against them, among nations that had passed away before them of jinn and humankind. Indeed, they were losers." Then: "Those who disbelieved said, 'Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that you may prevail.' So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment, and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do. That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire; for them therein is the abode of eternity, as a recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs." Then: "And those who disbelieved will say, 'Our Lord, show us those two who led us astray of the jinn and humankind; we will place them under our feet so that they will be among the lowest.'"

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the severe threat in this world and the Hereafter upon the disbelief of those disbelievers, He followed it with mention of the cause for which they fell into that disbelief. So He said: "And We appointed for them companions." On this there are several issues.

**The first issue:** The author of *al-Sihah* (al-Jawhari) said: one says *qayyadtu al-rajul muqayadah*, meaning I exchanged goods with the man; and they are two *qayyidan* (exchangers), as one says *bayyi'an* (two sellers). And *qayyada Allahu fulanan* means He brought him to him and brought it to him. From this is His saying: "And We appointed for them companions."

**The second issue:** Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued with this verse that He, exalted is He, wills disbelief from the disbeliever. They said: He, exalted is He, mentioned that He appointed for them those companions, and He knew that when He appointed for them those companions, they would make falsehood attractive to them. Whoever does an act and knows that this act will lead to an effect without doubt, the doer of that act must necessarily intend that effect. Thus it is established that when He appointed for them companions, He willed from them that disbelief. Al-Jubba'i (Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i) answered this by saying: If He willed the disobediences from them, they would be obedient by performing them, since the one who does what another wills from him must be obedient to him. And [he said] that His saying "And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me" (al-Dhariyat 56) indicates that He did not will from them except worship. Thus it is established by this that He, exalted is He, did not will disobediences from them. As for this verse, we say: He, exalted is He, did not say "And We appointed for them companions in order that they would make attractive to them," but He said "so they made attractive to them." So He appointed the companions for them in the sense that He brought each person to another of his kind; so He appointed one of the spouses for the other, the rich for the poor, and the poor for the rich. Then He, exalted is He, explained that some of them make disobediences attractive to others.

Know that the argument of our companions is what we mentioned: whoever does an act and knows with certainty that this act leads to an effect, the doer of that act is willing that effect. Here, Allah, exalted is He, appointed those companions for them, and He knew that when He appointed those companions for them, they would fall into that disbelief and misguidance. What al-Jubba'i mentioned does not repel this. As for his saying: "If Allah willed disobediences from them, they would be obedient to Allah by performing them," we say: If whoever does what another wills were obedient to him, it would necessarily follow that Allah would be obedient to His servants when they do what they will; and it is known that this is false. Moreover, this is a verbal reductio: it is said, if by obedience you mean that He did what He willed, then this is a reduction to the thing itself; and if you mean something else, then it must be explained so that it may be examined whether it is valid or not.

**The second issue (regarding the meaning):** They differed concerning the meaning of His saying "so they made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them." Al-Zajjaj mentioned two views concerning it:

The first: they made attractive to them what was before them of the matters of the Hereafter, that there is no resurrection, no Paradise, and no Fire; and what was behind them of the matters of this world; so they made it seem that the world is eternal, and that there is no agent or maker except the natures and the spheres.

The second: they made attractive to them their deeds which they perform and witness, and what was behind them, what they claim they know. Ibn Zayd expressed it, saying: they made attractive to them what had passed of their wicked deeds and what remained of their base deeds.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "And the Word became due against them among nations that had passed away before them of jinn and humankind; indeed, they were losers." Here His saying "among nations" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in "against them." The estimation is: the Word became due against them while they were included in the category of "nations" of those who came before them. "Indeed, they were losers." Our companions also argued with this, that He, exalted is He, informed that these ones "the Word became due against them." So if they were not disbelievers, this true word would turn into falsehood, this knowledge into ignorance, and this true report into a lie; and all of that is impossible, and what necessitates the impossible is impossible. Thus it is established that the issuing of faith from them and the non-issuing of disbelief from them is impossible.

Know that the discourse at the beginning of the surah began from His saying: "And they say: 'Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a veil; so act, indeed we are acting'" (Fussilat 5). Allah answered that doubt with various answers, and the discourse connected, some of it with the rest, up to this place. Then He related another doubt from them, saying: "And those who disbelieved said, 'Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that you may prevail.'" The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: it has been read "*wa-lghaw fihi*" with a fatha and a damma on the ghayn; one says *laghā yalghā* and *yalghū*. And *al-laghw* is what falls from speech that has no benefit in it.

Know that the people knew that the Qur'an is a complete speech in meaning and in wording, and that everyone who hears it becomes aware of the excellence of its words, his intellect comprehends its meanings, and his intellect decides that it is a true speech worthy of acceptance. So they devised a plan to prevent the people from listening to it. Some of them said to others: "Do not listen to this Qur'an" when it is recited, and occupy yourselves during its recitation by raising voices with nonsense, corrupt poetry and false words, so that you confuse the reciter, disturb him, and overpower his recitation. The Quraysh used to advise one another to do this. The intended meaning is: do during the recitation of the Qur'an what is idle and false, so that you take the recitation of the Qur'an out of being understood by the people; by this means you will overcome Muhammad (ﷺ). This is ignorance on their part, for at that moment they acknowledged that they were occupied with idle and false action, while Allah, exalted is He, supports Muhammad (ﷺ) by His grace.

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that, He threatened them with a severe punishment, saying: "So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment." This is because the word *dhawq* (tasting) is only mentioned for a small quantity which is brought for the purpose of testing. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned that this tasting is a severe punishment; so if its small part is a severe punishment, how will the large part of it be? Then He said: "and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do." They differed concerning it: most of them said: the intended meaning is the recompense of the badness of their deeds. Al-Hasan said: rather, the intended meaning is that He does not recompense them for the good of their deeds, because they nullified them with disbelief, so those good deeds were lost from them, and there remained with them only the ugly and false deeds; therefore they obtained nothing but the recompense of the evil deeds.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire." The meaning: when He said in the previous verse "and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do," He explained that this worst which was made the recompense of the enemies of Allah is the Fire.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "For them therein is the abode of eternity." That is, for them within the category of the Fire is the abode of evil deeds specified for them, which is the abode of everlasting punishment for them. "The recompense of the enemies of Allah is the Fire; for them..." That is, a recompense for what they used to make noise during the recitation. He called it denial (*judud*) because, when they knew that the Qur'an reached the limit of miraculousness, they feared that if people heard it they would believe in it, so they devised that corrupt method. This indicates that they knew it to be miraculous, but they denied it out of envy.

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained that what led them to disbelief, which necessitates the severe punishment, was sitting with evil companions, He explained that the disbelievers, when they fall into the severe punishment, will say: "Our Lord, show us those two who led us astray of the jinn and humankind." The reason for mentioning these two categories is that the devil is of two kinds: jinn and human. He, exalted is He, said: "And thus We appointed for every prophet an enemy: devils of humankind and jinn" (al-An'am 112), and He said: "Who whispers in the breasts of people, of the jinn and of humankind" (al-Nas 5-6). It has been said that they are Iblis and Qabil, because disbelief is the way (*sunnah*) of Iblis, and killing without right is the way of Qabil.

It has been read "*arna*" with a sukun on the ra' because of the heaviness of the kasra, as they say "*fakhdh*" for "*fakhidh*" (thigh). It has been said its meaning is: give us those two who led us astray. They related from al-Khalil that when you say "*arini thawbaka*" with a kasra, the meaning is: show me your garment (cause me to see it); and when you say it with a sukun, it is a request for giving, meaning: give me your garment.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "We will place them under our feet." Muqatil said: they will be lower than us in the Fire. "So that they will be among the lowest." Al-Zajjaj said: so that they will be in the lowest level (*al-darak al-asfal*) of the Fire.

One of my students, who inclined toward philosophy (*al-hikmah*), used to say: the intended meaning of the two who lead astray is desire (*al-shahwah*) and anger (*al-ghadab*), and the allusion to them is in the story of the angels with His saying: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it and sheds blood?" (al-Baqarah 30). Then he said: the intended meaning of His saying "We will place them under our feet" is: O our Lord, help us until we place desire and anger under the feet of the sacred essence of the soul. The intended meaning of their being under its feet is that they are subjected to the sacred soul and obedient to it, and that they are not supervisors over it or dominating it.

So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment, and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do. That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire; for them therein is the abode of eternity, as a recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs." Then: "And those who disbelieved will say, 'Our Lord, show us those two who led us astray of the jinn and humankind; we will place them under our feet so that they will be among the lowest.'"

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the severe threat in this world and the Hereafter upon the disbelief of those disbelievers, He followed it with mention of the cause for which they fell into that disbelief. So He said: "And We appointed for them companions." On this there are several issues.

**The first issue:** The author of *al-Sihah* (al-Jawhari) said: one says *qayyadtu al-rajul muqayadah*, meaning I exchanged goods with the man; and they are two *qayyidan* (exchangers), as one says *bayyi'an* (two sellers). And *qayyada Allahu fulanan* means He brought him to him and brought it to him. From this is His saying: "And We appointed for them companions."

**The second issue:** Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued with this verse that He, exalted is He, wills disbelief from the disbeliever. They said: He, exalted is He, mentioned that He appointed for them those companions, and He knew that when He appointed for them those companions, they would make falsehood attractive to them. Whoever does an act and knows that this act will lead to an effect without doubt, the doer of that act must necessarily intend that effect. Thus it is established that when He appointed for them companions, He willed from them that disbelief. Al-Jubba'i (Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i) answered this by saying: If He willed the disobediences from them, they would be obedient by performing them, since the one who does what another wills from him must be obedient to him. And [he said] that His saying "And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me" (al-Dhariyat 56) indicates that He did not will from them except worship. Thus it is established by this that He, exalted is He, did not will disobediences from them. As for this verse, we say: He, exalted is He, did not say "And We appointed for them companions in order that they would make attractive to them," but He said "so they made attractive to them." So He appointed the companions for them in the sense that He brought each person to another of his kind; so He appointed one of the spouses for the other, the rich for the poor, and the poor for the rich. Then He, exalted is He, explained that some of them make disobediences attractive to others.

Know that the argument of our companions is what we mentioned: whoever does an act and knows with certainty that this act leads to an effect, the doer of that act is willing that effect. Here, Allah, exalted is He, appointed those companions for them, and He knew that when He appointed those companions for them, they would fall into that disbelief and misguidance. What al-Jubba'i mentioned does not repel this. As for his saying: "If Allah willed disobediences from them, they would be obedient to Allah by performing them," we say: If whoever does what another wills were obedient to him, it would necessarily follow that Allah would be obedient to His servants when they do what they will; and it is known that this is false. Moreover, this is a verbal reductio: it is said, if by obedience you mean that He did what He willed, then this is a reduction to the thing itself; and if you mean something else, then it must be explained so that it may be examined whether it is valid or not.

**The second issue (regarding the meaning):** They differed concerning the meaning of His saying "so they made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them." Al-Zajjaj mentioned two views concerning it:

The first: they made attractive to them what was before them of the matters of the Hereafter, that there is no resurrection, no Paradise, and no Fire; and what was behind them of the matters of this world; so they made it seem that the world is eternal, and that there is no agent or maker except the natures and the spheres.

The second: they made attractive to them their deeds which they perform and witness, and what was behind them, what they claim they know. Ibn Zayd expressed it, saying: they made attractive to them what had passed of their wicked deeds and what remained of their base deeds.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "And the Word became due against them among nations that had passed away before them of jinn and humankind; indeed, they were losers." Here His saying "among nations" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in "against them." The estimation is: the Word became due against them while they were included in the category of "nations" of those who came before them. "Indeed, they were losers." Our companions also argued with this, that He, exalted is He, informed that these ones "the Word became due against them." So if they were not disbelievers, this true word would turn into falsehood, this knowledge into ignorance, and this true report into a lie; and all of that is impossible, and what necessitates the impossible is impossible. Thus it is established that the issuing of faith from them and the non-issuing of disbelief from them is impossible.

Know that the discourse at the beginning of the surah began from His saying: "And they say: 'Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a veil; so act, indeed we are acting'" (Fussilat 5). Allah answered that doubt with various answers, and the discourse connected, some of it with the rest, up to this place. Then He related another doubt from them, saying: "And those who disbelieved said, 'Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that you may prevail.'" The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: it has been read "*wa-lghaw fihi*" with a fatha and a damma on the ghayn; one says *laghā yalghā* and *yalghū*. And *al-laghw* is what falls from speech that has no benefit in it.

Know that the people knew that the Qur'an is a complete speech in meaning and in wording, and that everyone who hears it becomes aware of the excellence of its words, his intellect comprehends its meanings, and his intellect decides that it is a true speech worthy of acceptance. So they devised a plan to prevent the people from listening to it. Some of them said to others: "Do not listen to this Qur'an" when it is recited, and occupy yourselves during its recitation by raising voices with nonsense, corrupt poetry and false words, so that you confuse the reciter, disturb him, and overpower his recitation. The Quraysh used to advise one another to do this. The intended meaning is: do during the recitation of the Qur'an what is idle and false, so that you take the recitation of the Qur'an out of being understood by the people; by this means you will overcome Muhammad (ﷺ). This is ignorance on their part, for at that moment they acknowledged that they were occupied with idle and false action, while Allah, exalted is He, supports Muhammad (ﷺ) by His grace.

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that, He threatened them with a severe punishment, saying: "So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment." This is because the word *dhawq* (tasting) is only mentioned for a small quantity which is brought for the purpose of testing. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned that this tasting is a severe punishment; so if its small part is a severe punishment, how will the large part of it be? Then He said: "and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do." They differed concerning it: most of them said: the intended meaning is the recompense of the badness of their deeds. Al-Hasan said: rather, the intended meaning is that He does not recompense them for the good of their deeds, because they nullified them with disbelief, so those good deeds were lost from them, and there remained with them only the ugly and false deeds; therefore they obtained nothing but the recompense of the evil deeds.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire." The meaning: when He said in the previous verse "and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do," He explained that this worst which was made the recompense of the enemies of Allah is the Fire.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "For them therein is the abode of eternity." That is, for them within the category of the Fire is the abode of evil deeds specified for them, which is the abode of everlasting punishment for them. "The recompense of the enemies of Allah is the Fire; for them..." That is, a recompense for what they used to make noise during the recitation. He called it denial (*judud*) because, when they knew that the Qur'an reached the limit of miraculousness, they feared that if people heard it they would believe in it, so they devised that corrupt method. This indicates that they knew it to be miraculous, but they denied it out of envy.

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained that what led them to disbelief, which necessitates the severe punishment, was sitting with evil companions, He explained that the disbelievers, when they fall into the severe punishment, will say: "Our Lord, show us those two who led us astray of the jinn and humankind." The reason for mentioning these two categories is that the devil is of two kinds: jinn and human. He, exalted is He, said: "And thus We appointed for every prophet an enemy: devils of humankind and jinn" (al-An'am 112), and He said: "Who whispers in the breasts of people, of the jinn and of humankind" (al-Nas 5-6). It has been said that they are Iblis and Qabil, because disbelief is the way (*sunnah*) of Iblis, and killing without right is the way of Qabil.

It has been read "*arna*" with a sukun on the ra' because of the heaviness of the kasra, as they say "*fakhdh*" for "*fakhidh*" (thigh). It has been said its meaning is: give us those two who led us astray. They related from al-Khalil that when you say "*arini thawbaka*" with a kasra, the meaning is: show me your garment (cause me to see it); and when you say it with a sukun, it is a request for giving, meaning: give me your garment.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "We will place them under our feet." Muqatil said: they will be lower than us in the Fire. "So that they will be among the lowest." Al-Zajjaj said: so that they will be in the lowest level (*al-darak al-asfal*) of the Fire.

One of my students, who inclined toward philosophy (*al-hikmah*), used to say: the intended meaning of the two who lead astray is desire (*al-shahwah*) and anger (*al-ghadab*), and the allusion to them is in the story of the angels with His saying: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it and sheds blood?" (al-Baqarah 30). Then he said: the intended meaning of His saying "We will place them under our feet" is: O our Lord, help us until we place desire and anger under the feet of the sacred essence of the soul. The intended meaning of their being under its feet is that they are subjected to the sacred soul and obedient to it, and that they are not supervisors over it or dominating it.

Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast (الِاسْتِقامَة, istiqamah), the angels descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, and rejoice in the Paradise you were promised." We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. For you therein is what your souls desire, and for you therein is what you ask for. As a welcome from the Forgiving, the Merciful.

Know that when He, exalted is He, had dwelt at length on the threat, He followed it with this noble promise. This is a subtle arrangement on which the whole of the Qur'an revolves. We have mentioned repeatedly that perfections are of three kinds: the psychic (al-nafsaniyyah), the bodily (al-badaniyyah), and the external (al-kharijiyyah). The highest of these ranks is the psychic, the middle is the bodily, and the lowest is the external. We have also mentioned that psychic perfections are confined to two types: certain knowledge (al-'ilm al-yaqini) and righteous action (al-'amal al-salih). The people of verification (ahl al-tahqiq) said: the perfection of a human being lies in knowing the Truth for its own sake and the good for the sake of acting upon it. The head and chief of certain knowledge is the knowledge of Allah, and to this points His saying: ﴿Indeed those who say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾. The head and chief of righteous deeds is that a person be upright in the middle, not inclining to either extreme of excess or deficiency, as He said: ﴿Thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], and He also said: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾. To this points His saying in this verse: ﴿then remained steadfast﴾.

I have heard that a reciter recited this verse in the assembly of al-'Abbadi, and al-'Abbadi said: "The resurrection is in the resurrection, according to the measure of steadfastness." Knowing this, we say: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remained steadfast﴾ does not mean merely saying it with the tongue, because that alone does not produce steadfastness. Since steadfastness was mentioned after that saying, we know that the saying was accompanied by complete certainty and true knowledge. Knowing this, we say: concerning steadfastness there are two opinions:

The first: it means steadfastness in the religion, in monotheism (al-tawhid), and in knowledge.

The second: it means steadfastness in righteous deeds.

As for the first opinion, there are several expressions on it. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Then remained steadfast," i.e., they did not turn to any god other than Him. Ibn 'Abbas said in some narrations: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, because Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, fell into severe kinds of affliction and trial, yet he never changed at all from his religion. He was the one who said: ﴿Our Lord is Allah﴾, and he remained steadfast upon it, not changing for any cause whatsoever.

I say: there are other aspects in this, namely that whoever affirms that this world has a God, there remain for him other stations. The first of them is that he should not go so far in affirmation as to end in anthropomorphism (al-tashbih), but should remain on the straight line dividing anthropomorphism from negation (al-ta'til). Likewise he must remain on the straight line dividing compulsion (al-jabr) from divine decree (al-qadar). Similarly, in hope and despair, he must remain on the straight line. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Indeed those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remained steadfast﴾. As for the second opinion, which is that we understand steadfastness as the performing of righteous deeds, this is the view of a large group of the Companions and the Successors (al-tabi'un). They said: this is preferable, so that His saying ﴿Indeed those who say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ encompasses the saying and the belief, and His saying ﴿then remained steadfast﴾ encompasses the righteous deeds.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿the angels descend upon them﴾. It was said: at the time of death. It was also said: at three stations: at death, in the grave, and at the resurrection until the Final Day. ﴿Do not fear﴾: here "an" (أنْ) is in the sense of "ay" (أيْ, that is), or it is the lightened form (مُخَفَّفَة) of the heavy "anna" (أنَّ), and its original is "bi-annahu la takhafu," where the "ha'" is the pronoun of the matter (ضَمِيرُ الشَّأْنِ). Know that the ultimate aim in safeguarding interests is the repelling of harms and the securing of benefits. It is well known that repelling harm takes precedence over securing benefit. Harm either occurs in the future, or in the present, or in the past. Here there is a subtle rational point: the future precedes the present, and the present precedes the past. For a thing that has not yet existed and whose occurrence is anticipated is future; when it exists it becomes present; when it perishes and passes away after that, it becomes past. Also, the future draws nearer to attainment every hour, while the past becomes further from attainment in every state. For this reason the poet said:

"May what you desire never cease to be nearer than tomorrow,
and may what you fear never cease to be further than yesterday."

Since this is established, harms anticipated to occur in the future deserve repelling more than past harms. Also, fear (al-khawf) is the pain of the heart caused by the anticipation of harm in the future, and grief (al-hazn) is the pain of the heart caused by the loss of a benefit that existed in the past. Given this, repelling fear takes precedence over repelling the grief that arises from sorrow. Knowing this, we say: He, exalted is He, informed about the angels that at the outset they announce that there is no fear upon you concerning what you will encounter of the states of the Resurrection. Then they announce that there is no grief upon you concerning what has escaped you of the affairs of the world. When these two matters are attained, harms and hardships have wholly vanished.

Then, after this is complete, they give them the good news (yubashsharun) of the attainment of benefits, and this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and rejoice in the Paradise you were promised﴾. If it is asked: glad tidings (al-bisharah) is the first report of the attainment of a benefit. When a man reports to someone that a benefit has been attained, and then reports a second time that it has been attained, the second report is an informing and not glad tidings. The believer often hears good tidings of goodness, so when the believer hears this report from the angels, it should be an informing and not glad tidings. What is the reason for calling this report glad tidings? We answer: the believer hears that whoever is a believing and pious person has Paradise. As for one who has never heard at all that he is among the people of Paradise, when he hears this speech from the angels, it is an informing of a great benefit, and since it is the first report of that, it is glad tidings.

Know that this speech indicates that the believer, at death, in the grave, and at the resurrection, is not panicked by the terrors and by severe dread, but is secure of heart and tranquil of breast. For His saying ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾ conveys the negation of fear and grief in an absolute sense.

Then He, exalted is He, informed about the angels that they said to the believers: ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾. This stands in contrast to what He mentioned in the threat against the disbelievers, when He said: ﴿And We appointed for them companions﴾ [Fussilat: 25]. The meaning of their being allies to the believers is that the angels have influences upon human spirits through inspirations and certain unveilings (al-mukashafat), and through true stations, just as the devils have influences upon spirits by casting whisperings into them and presenting falsehoods to them.

In sum, the angels being allies to pure and purified spirits arises from many aspects that are known to the people of unveilings and direct witnessing. They say: just as that allegiance existed in the world, it will remain in the Hereafter, for those bonds are intrinsic, necessary, and not subject to cessation. Rather, after death they become even stronger and more lasting. This is because the essence of the soul is of the kind of the angels. It is like a spark in relation to fire, or a drop in relation to the sea. The bodily attachments are what intervene between it and the angels, as he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Were it not that the devils hover over the hearts of the children of Adam, they would look upon the dominion of the heavens." When the bodily attachments and bodily management are removed, the covering and the obstruction are gone, so the effect joins the influencer, the drop joins the sea, and the spark joins the sun. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾.

[Page 107]

Then He said: ﴿For you therein is what your souls desire, and for you therein is what you ask for﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿what you ask for﴾ means what you wish for, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is what they ask for﴾ [Ya-Sin: 57]. If it is asked: according to this explanation, there is no difference between His saying ﴿For you therein is what your souls desire﴾ and His saying ﴿For you therein is what you ask for﴾. We answer: in my view, the closer interpretation is that His saying ﴿For you therein is what your souls desire﴾ refers to the bodily Paradise, and His saying ﴿For you therein is what you ask for﴾ refers to the spiritual Paradise mentioned in His saying: ﴿Their call therein is, "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein is peace; and the last of their call is, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Yunus: 10].

* * *

Its placement is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). The gnostics (al-'arifun) said: this verse indicates that all these mentioned things are in the manner of a nuzul. When the Generous gives the nuzul, He must then send precious robes of honour after it, and those precious robes are none other than the felicities attained at the vision, the manifestation, and the complete unveiling.
